message.content:
Task: a thorough novelty/crowding check for a planned preregistered study, and a list of the 5 closest papers with exact details. Write results to ~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper/scoping/anchoring_novelty_check.md and return a summary.

Planned study: Using the Open Anchoring Quest (OpAQ) dataset (Röseler et al. 2022, J Open Psychol Data, doi 10.5334/jopd.67; OSF ygnvb; 412 anchoring items, 96 studies, 88,914 trial-level estimates), test how the PROPORTIONAL anchoring index (AI = difference between high-anchor and low-anchor central estimates / difference between the anchors; Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995 style) changes with anchor extremity (anchor distance relative to the true value and/or to uncertainty about the quantity), at the item level, and compare against predictions simulated from four process models: resource-rational adjustment (Lieder, Griffiths, Huys & Goodman 2018, Psychon Bull Rev, two papers), anchor integration model (Turner & Schley 2016, Cogn Psychol), insufficient adjustment to plausible range (Epley & Gilovich 2006), selective accessibility / plausibility (Mussweiler & Strack 1999; Wegener, Petty et al. 2001; Strack & Mussweiler 1997). Background: the meta-analysis on OpAQ (Röseler & Schütz, "Hanging the anchor off a new ship", PsyArXiv doi 10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn) regressed Hedges' g on mean relative anchor distance and found a positive nonlinear relationship; it called for a unitless relative-adjustment metric. A full text is at /tmp/jdmsim/hanging.txt and the OpAQ data paper at /tmp/jdmsim/opaq.txt.

Do NOT download or open any data files (blinding rule). Read papers only.

Check specifically:
1. Has Röseler & Schütz been published in a journal since (find the version of record and whether the distance analysis changed)? Are there 2023–2026 papers reusing OpAQ (OpenAlex: works citing 10.5334/jopd.67 and citing the meta-analysis preprint; OpenAlex keys: run `set -a; source ~/.claude/api_keys.env; set +a`; use `&api_key=$OPENALEX_API_KEY`; rotate across `$OPENALEX_API_KEYS` if you hit quota)? Summarise what each did.
2. Has anyone tested the anchoring INDEX (proportional adjustment) as a function of anchor extremity across many items, or fitted process models to multi-study anchoring data? Check: Schley & Weingarten (Management Science 2026?, doi 10.1287/mnsc.2023.03238; and PsyArXiv teq7k); Bystranowski et al. 2021 (anchoring in legal judgments meta-analysis); Chapman & Johnson 1994 "The limits of anchoring"; Thorsteinson 2011; Wegener et al. 2001 & 2010; Mussweiler & Strack 2001; Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995; Lieder et al. 2018a/b; Turner & Schley 2016; Schultze, Rakotoarisoa & Schulz-Hardt 2015 (distance between initial estimate and advice); Simmons, LeBoeuf & Nelson 2010; Frederick & Mochon 2012 (scale distortion); Townson 2019; Bahník & Strack; Harris et al. 2019; Shanks et al. 2020; Röseler et al. 2023/2024 papers; any 2024–2026 computational anchoring model papers (search "anchoring" + "computational model" / "Bayesian" / "resource-rational" / "sampling" 2022–2026).
3. For each of the 5 closest papers: full citation, DOI verified via https://api.crossref.org/works/<DOI> (title and first author must match), what they did precisely (design, measure, key numeric result), and what our planned study would add relative to it.
4. Any direct quantitative predictions in the literature for how the anchoring index varies with extremity (e.g., Jacowitz & Kahneman found AI ~ .49 with 15th/85th percentile anchors; any studies with very extreme/implausible anchors reporting AI or proportional adjustment — e.g., Strack & Mussweiler 1997 implausible anchors, Chapman & Johnson 1994, Wegener 2001, Mussweiler & Strack 2000 — give numbers).
Verdict at the end: NOT DONE / PARTLY DONE / DONE, with confidence and what is still open.

# About me

I am Lukas, a social psychologist, meta-scientist and open science advocate, who mostly uses you to get research done and build the tooling that supports it (in addition to teaching support). I have a solid understanding of software development and infrastructure, but am no expert, so that I will often need clear recommendations and explanations. Most of what I build is tooling for one-off projects, most is not intended to be production-ready or backwards-compatible. Feel free to clarify that project-by-project, but generally lean, efficient and clear code is more important than any backwards-compatible shim or edge-case handling.

I also regularly need your help in writing. For that, and in code, the most annoying failure mode is when history leaks in - when a text argues against its previous versions, or code comments are more about what is gone than about what the curent code does. Here, writing and reviewing outputs from the perspective of a new reader is essential.

# How to work

## Delegation: Fable as Orchestrator

When the session model is Fable, work **orchestrator-first**: plan, delegate substantive work to cheaper subagents, then review and synthesize. Fable itself keeps task decomposition, design decisions and judgment calls, reviewing subagent output, final synthesis and user-facing writing, plus edits so trivial that delegating would take longer. Everything else — implementation, broad searches, analyses, mechanical batch work — goes to subagents by default.

## Using sub-agents

- **Default subagent model: Opus** (`model: "opus"` on the Agent tool / workflow `agent()` calls). Drop to Sonnet or Haiku for clearly mechanical, high-volume steps; reserve Fable-model subagents for only the hardest verify/judge stages.
- **codex CLI** — via the `codex-delegate` skill: (a) independent second opinions and code review (read-only), and (b) self-contained implementation tasks with `--approve-for-me` — good for parallel, independent work streams.
- **agy CLI** (Antigravity; Gemini 3.x + others, `agy models` lists them) — via the `agy-delegate` skill: (a) **large-context reads** — digesting big files, PDFs, logs, or datasets that would bloat Claude context — and (b) **cross-model second opinions**.
- **In Workflow scripts**, reach codex/agy through cheap relay agents: `agent(relayPrompt, {model: 'sonnet', effort: 'low'})`, where `relayPrompt` says "You are a relay agent. Pass the following payload prompt through the `codex-delegate` [or `agy-delegate`] skill, wait for its answer, and return its answer verbatim as your final message; do not answer the payload yourself." followed by the payload, the working directory, and mode/model choices. The relay is pure transport — the skill holds the CLI recipe; keep payload prompts self-contained. Make sure the agents run the request in the foreground, with generous timeout as a subagent that backgrounds codex and waits on monitors/notifications often never gets resumed, stranding the finished answer on disk. If a codex-relay subagent goes quiet, don't wait for it — `ls` for the output file and read it directly.
- Delegation must not degrade quality: give subagents complete, self-contained prompts with all needed context and file paths, and verify load-bearing results yourself rather than trusting a subagent's summary.
- Assign clear ownership of every delegated write target. When two or more agents or processes may write the same file, branch, key, or state object at the same time, give each an independent write target. Different fields in one state file are still one shared target. Merge outputs only when reading or reporting them. If one shared target is required, use one writer, a lock, or sequential phases. Scratch files count as write targets: parallel subagents share one scratchpad directory, so tell each to name its temporary scripts and data after its own task (`scratch_refs_3.py`, not `scratch_build.py`) — otherwise one agent overwrites and executes another's file mid-run.

## Build the Small Tool

When work includes repeated edits, data processing, an analysis, a migration, or a non-trivial check, build the smallest tool that does or verifies it. Use a script, query, generator, codemod, or skill as appropriate. The tool is a reviewable artifact that someone can read and rerun.

Work through one unit to establish the recipe. Build the tool. Run it on that unit and compare its result with the hand-produced result.

Use one deterministic pass when it can handle all units. Delegate building or reviewing that tool when needed; do not assign agents to hand-apply each unit. For delegated work, put the recipe, verification steps, and files agents must not edit in one skill outside their write scope.

Commit the tool when future work will need it.

## Codex CLI (second-opinion / review)

When invoking `codex` non-interactively (e.g. for a second opinion or code review), follow this exact recipe:

1. **Feed the prompt via stdin, with `-` as the prompt arg:**

  replacement — heredoc rewrites hide the diff.

  file isn't cached locally; retry once before treating as an error.

In my research, I often need your help with statistical analyses. Make sure these are appropriate and robust. If we change direction and another analysis approach becomes more appropriate, we should generally change track (unless compute cost is very high).

When reproducing, replicating, or re-analysing a previous study, match the original as faithfully as possible by DEFAULT — same sample inclusion rules, same variables, same operationalisations, same model. not a narrated story. The test: could someone who did not watch the work act on
each sentence without rereading it or asking what it refers to? For that, largely use

Concretely:

1. **Lead with the fact, not the framing.** "Added a manifest hash check at Stage 3

2. **No process narration.** Skip who suggested what, what was declined, what an
   agent "pushed back" on, and why a fix is "worth noting". Report the decision and

3. **Resolve every reference in place.** Never write "#17", "the #8 question",
   or a label coined earlier in the session without saying what
   it is: "finding #17 (rule-pick caching during outages)". Assume the reader has
   no memory of the earlier conversation.
4. **One clause, one fact.** No sentences that stack a claim, its justification,
   and a contrast with an alternative separated by dashes. Split them.
5. **Structure over prose for multi-item status.** Three or more parallel items

   with a bolded label per item, not woven into paragraphs.

   because", "the honest answer is", "notably". State the fact; let it carry its
   own weight.

   so nothing waiting on the user is buried mid-paragraph.

training. Do not dumb things down or pad explanations — just prefer the plain term
when one exists and carries the same meaning: "check before writing" over
"TOCTOU-safe", "lookup table" over "hashmap semantics", "partly overwritten file" 
over "torn write". When a term of art is genuinely the precise word (idempotent, race condition), 
use it, and add a five-word gloss in parentheses the first time it appears in a session if the
meaning isn't clear from context. Never use jargon as compression when a plain
phrase is barely longer.

- `academic/wallrich_academic_style_guide.md` — voice, spelling, hedging, banned vocabulary, sentence structure, citations, footnotes. Section-specific detail in `academic/sections/{introduction,methods,discussion}.md`. 
- `teaching/wallrich_teaching_style_guide.md` — slides, workshops, handouts, and other audience-facing material.

1. **Always look up DOIs** via the Crossref API (`https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic={url_encoded_reference}`) or web search. Never guess a DOI.
2. **Verify each DOI resolves** by fetching `https://api.crossref.org/works/{DOI}` and checking the returned metadata matches.
3. If a DOI cannot be found, **omit the DOI field** rather than inventing one.
4. For author names, titles, and publication details: verify against Crossref metadata or the publisher's website. Do not rely on memory for these details.

1. **State the estimate up front**: (price per token × tokens/call × number of calls), and say it out loud before running. Get confirmation for anything beyond a few dollars.
2. **Watch reasoning/thinking models**: a thinking model bills its hidden reasoning tokens as output and can cost ~10-30× a plain model for the same task. Prefer non-thinking models when output is short (e.g. a small JSON), and cap/lower the reasoning budget when a thinking model is needed.
3. **Use the cheapest viable provider/routing**: on OpenRouter pin cheapest-provider routing WITH a performance floor — `provider: {sort: "price", preferred_min_throughput: 40}` (tok/s; `preferred_max_latency` also exists) — because a pure price sort can route to a host queuing requests for minutes each. 4. **Capture actual spend**: request usage/cost in the response and report it, so estimates can be checked against reality. If a run is substantially more expensive than estimated, stop and re-confirm.

## Backward Compatibility and Tests

Ensure core functionality is covered by tests, but avoid slop and large sets of smoke tests. Less is more.

## Make Reruns Safe

For every command, lifecycle step, or processing loop that may be retried, restarted, or interrupted, design it to reach the correct end state after any number of runs. This includes file-writing scripts and batched external calls.

Check two cases: a second run after success, and a run after interruption at each step. If a prior run may have left partial or stale state, inspect it before continuing. Reuse completed work, repair incomplete outputs, and remove artifacts or locks only after confirming that they are stale.

When deciding whether work is complete, compare stable content or identifiers, not file count or creation order.

Any command written for me to run should work as-is when pasted into my shell from the
project root. No placeholders I have to resolve, and no interpreter or tool that is
not on my PATH — I copy what you write and run it.

In practice this means naming the project's own interpreter or entry point rather than
a generic one: `.venv/bin/python -m extract.export --release abc123`, not
`python -m extract.export ...`.

Always verify that changes work (run tests, render outputs, check results) before presenting them as complete. Don't leave the user with "to verify, do X" — do it yourself.

When modifying code that produces visual output (plots, charts, UI components), always render and visually inspect the result before presenting the change as complete. Never declare formatting fixes "done" based on code logic alone, except for internal-facing HTML pages. For these, trust your judgement.

When editing something that is deployed (e.g. a GH page), deploying it is part of the task. When the edit is trivial, deploy. When it needs my review, ask for confirmation - but never let me guess whether the latest update is live.

# Working with git

## Committing: Fetch Before Building a Commit Stack

`git fetch` and check `main...origin/main` BEFORE committing, especially when building a stack. 
Also check `git log` for local commits that appeared since the session started (a collaborator or another session may have committed from the same checkout); verify shared files weren't clobbered before stacking on top.

## Parallel Agents in Git Worktrees

- **Merge by the agent's merge-base, never against current main/master.** An agent branches from
  the state that existed when it started, so `git diff main <branch>` carries *deletions of
  everything merged since*; applying it silently reverts already-merged work, with nothing in the
  output to indicate it. Use
  `git diff $(git merge-base main <branch>) <branch> -- <file>` to get only the agent's own
  changes, and re-verify previously merged work after each merge — not just the piece just landed.
- **Remove each worktree as it lands, not at the end.** Each is a full checkout; a wide wave can
  fill the disk mid-session, and worktree creation then fails with "No space left on device".

contaminate stdout. Write to a file first (`gws … --format json > out.json 2>err.log`),
`head -c 300` it to confirm it is JSON, then parse. Pass API arguments through
`--params '<JSON>'`, not as flags or positionals. After parsing any API response,
print the top-level keys before indexing into them.

## Sanity-Check Prompts

If a user prompt seems unrelated to the current project/working directory, or references files, concepts, or protocols that don't exist in the codebase, ask the user to confirm before proceeding. They may be in the wrong folder.

## Scratch / Throwaway Files

Name temporary or throwaway files with a `scratch` prefix (e.g. `scratch.py`, `scratch_notes.md`, `scratch_test.js`). The `/wrap` end-of-session skill detects files matching `scratch*` and offers to commit or delete them during wrap-up.

## Recurring Corrections Become Mechanisms

When the same correction or unexpected failure recurs, encode the fix in a mechanism: a test, hook, lint rule, validation step, safer code default, or automation. Apply the mechanism now and remove the duplicate prose.

Use the strongest mechanism available. Prefer a restriction that makes an invalid state impossible. If that is not possible, use a lint or CI check, a shared helper, or a runtime check.

Keep a prose rule only when it requires judgment. State the decision and the failure mode it prevents.

## Statistical analyses

In my research, I often need your help with statistical analyses. Make sure these are appropriate and robust. If we change direction and another analysis approach becomes more appropriate, we should generally change track (unless compute cost is very high).

### Reproducing / Replicating Prior Analyses

When reproducing, replicating, or re-analysing a previous study, match the original as faithfully as possible by DEFAULT — same sample inclusion rules, same variables, same operationalisations, same model. Do NOT introduce deviations (different year ranges, team/group-size filters, measures, controls, transformations) for convenience, tractability, or unstated preference. If a deviation is genuinely warranted (e.g. to fix a confound, handle censoring, or reduce compute), STOP and flag it explicitly, explain why, and get agreement before building on it. When a deviation is kept, state it and its justification plainly in the writeup and flag it briefly in the code.

# Writing

## Status Reports and Summaries: Plain Over Clever

When reporting progress, findings, or decisions, write like a technical changelog,
not a narrated story. The test: could someone who did not watch the work act on
each sentence without rereading it or asking what it refers to? For that, largely use
ASD-STE100, but deviate where that increases clarity and readability.

Concretely:

1. **Lead with the fact, not the framing.** "Added a manifest hash check at Stage 3
   startup; hashing 300 MB takes 0.10 s" — not "The manifest binding is in,
   positioned with the other startup refusals, and the agent measured the cost
   rather than assuming it."
2. **No process narration.** Skip who suggested what, what was declined, what an
   agent "pushed back" on, and why a fix is "worth noting". Report the decision and
   its one-line reason; drop the story of how it was reached unless asked.
3. **Resolve every reference in place.** Never write "#17", "the #8 question",
   or a label coined earlier in the session without saying what
   it is: "finding #17 (rule-pick caching during outages)". Assume the reader has
   no memory of the earlier conversation.
4. **One clause, one fact.** No sentences that stack a claim, its justification,
   and a contrast with an alternative separated by dashes. Split them.
5. **Structure over prose for multi-item status.** Three or more parallel items
   (fixes applied, decisions pending, open questions) go in a list or short table
   with a bolded label per item, not woven into paragraphs.
6. **Ban editorializing connectors**: "which is the entire point", "worth noting
   because", "the honest answer is", "notably". State the fact; let it carry its
   own weight.
7. **Separate done / pending / needs-my-decision** into visibly distinct blocks,
   so nothing waiting on the user is buried mid-paragraph.

## Jargon: I Know the Concepts, Not the Vocabulary

I have a solid working understanding of programming and systems, but no formal CS
training. Do not dumb things down or pad explanations — just prefer the plain term
when one exists and carries the same meaning: "check before writing" over
"TOCTOU-safe", "lookup table" over "hashmap semantics", "partly overwritten file" 
over "torn write". When a term of art is genuinely the precise word (idempotent, race condition), 
use it, and add a five-word gloss in parentheses the first time it appears in a session if the
meaning isn't clear from context. Never use jargon as compression when a plain
phrase is barely longer.

## Style Guides

My written style guides live in `~/Documents/Coding/style_guides`:

- `academic/wallrich_academic_style_guide.md` — voice, spelling, hedging, banned vocabulary, sentence structure, citations, footnotes. Section-specific detail in `academic/sections/{introduction,methods,discussion}.md`. 
- `teaching/wallrich_teaching_style_guide.md` — slides, workshops, handouts, and other audience-facing material.

Read the relevant guide before drafting, revising, or reviewing my prose in that register, and before proposing additions to it.

## Statistical Results in Quarto/Rmd Reports

CRITICAL: NEVER write interpretive prose about statistical results you haven't seen. Produce the numbers first, read the rendered output, then write the text. The full conventions are in the `quarto-reporting` skill. Load it when creating or editing `.qmd` or `.Rmd` files.

## Academic References and DOIs

CRITICAL: NEVER fabricate DOIs, citation metadata, or reference details from memory. DOIs, author lists, titles, page numbers, and volume/issue numbers are exact identifiers — getting them wrong is worse than omitting them.

When creating references:
1. **Always look up DOIs** via the Crossref API (`https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic={url_encoded_reference}`) or web search. Never guess a DOI.
2. **Verify each DOI resolves** by fetching `https://api.crossref.org/works/{DOI}` and checking the returned metadata matches.
3. If a DOI cannot be found, **omit the DOI field** rather than inventing one.
4. For author names, titles, and publication details: verify against Crossref metadata or the publisher's website. Do not rely on memory for these details.

## Reading Academic Articles from HTML

When reading an academic article from an HTML page, ensure the page has fully loaded before extracting or searching its text, and confirm you are actually looking at the full text rather than just the abstract/landing view. A search that comes back empty can mean the content hasn't rendered yet, not that it isn't there. Take a screenshot to see what is actually on the page, before concluding a section is missing or treating the abstract as the whole article.

## Key failure mode - insufficient editing / drift

### The text has no memory of its drafts

Readers see only the final text, never its revision history. They do not know what an earlier draft said, what was wrong with it, or why a claim was softened or dropped. All external writing must read as a clean, self-contained statement of the *current* message, not as a reply to a previous version. Watch for "history leakage": phrasing that only makes sense against a framing the reader never saw. Tells include "not simply X", "rather than Y", "this is not the wrong variable", "to be fair", "the honest limits are narrower", "less a reprieve than a reminder", "we no longer…", and defensive hedges that rebut objections raised only in our own discussion. State the positive claim directly — say what the thing IS and what genuinely limits it, not what it is not relative to a draft.

This applies with full force to durable reference text: CLAUDE.md rules, code comments, docs, commit messages, skill files. A rule states the current fact ("GNU coreutils is on PATH"), never the story of its own correction — no "installed Jul 2026", "exists now", "no longer missing", "fixed since", "never assume X is absent". Those phrasings only make sense to someone who held the old, wrong belief; every future reader starts from the rule itself. Before saving any rule or comment, reread it as a stranger: if it reads as a rebuttal, rewrite it as the fact.

### When we agree to restructure, actually restart

If you and I agree to write a *fresh* draft or a new outline rather than edit the existing one, write it fresh from the agreed outline. Do not silently carry over the previous version's spine, ordering, emphasis, or lead just because it's already there — that is how an obsolete framing survives a "rewrite." Carry over only the verified facts, numbers and sources; treat the prior draft's structure as superseded unless we explicitly decide to keep a part of it.

# HTML files as a common output

Whenever you write long plans, proposals or report, assume HTML output as a default. It is more readable than md. When you need detailed feedback, include */html-comments*.

Link identifiers wherever they resolve: DOIs as `https://doi.org/…`, arXiv IDs as `https://arxiv.org/abs/…`, repos, issues, dataset accessions. Cited constructs (a named statistic, rubric or method) get a short hover gloss (`<abbr title="…">`) and a References section at the end.

Every standalone HTML file gets an emoji favicon as a `data:` URI, right after `<title>`:

```html
<link rel="icon" href="data:image/svg+xml,<svg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' viewBox='0 0 100 100'><text y='.9em' font-size='90'>🦸</text></svg>">
```

- Pick for the page's **topic**, never its type (no 📋 for every plan, 📊 for every
  report) — several are open at once and must be distinguishable. Keep it stable
  across edits to a file.
- Escape `#` as `%23`; keep double quotes outside, single quotes inside.
- Safari ignores SVG favicons: for participant- or reviewer-facing pages use
  `type="image/png"` with a base64 PNG (`base64 -i icon.png | tr -d '\n'`).

To open a webpage for the user, use the Bash tool to run `open <url>`. Do not use Claude artefacts by default. Keep scratch files local, deploy single collaborative files to surge.sh, and use GH pages for project-related files that are supposed to be shared.

# Working with APIs

## Keys

Reusable API keys live in `~/.claude/api_keys.env` (private to this machine, never shared). Load them with `set -a; source ~/.claude/api_keys.env; set +a` before running a script that needs them. 

Holds OpenAlex keys: `OPENALEX_API_KEY` (default) and `OPENALEX_API_KEYS` (comma-separated list of all keys). Rotate when quota is exhausted.

## Model Versions

Never assume that a model version I specify does not exist just because it's newer than your training data. If you're uncertain whether a model exists, search the web to verify. Never silently substitute an older version.

## API Cost Management

CRITICAL: Before launching any substantial paid-API job (batch LLM calls, large embedding/generation runs, anything looping over many items), explicitly estimate and confirm the cost with me *before* spending:
1. **State the estimate up front**: (price per token × tokens/call × number of calls), and say it out loud before running. Get confirmation for anything beyond a few dollars.
2. **Watch reasoning/thinking models**: a thinking model bills its hidden reasoning tokens as output and can cost ~10-30× a plain model for the same task. Prefer non-thinking models when output is short (e.g. a small JSON), and cap/lower the reasoning budget when a thinking model is needed.
3. **Use the cheapest viable provider/routing**: on OpenRouter pin cheapest-provider routing WITH a performance floor — `provider: {sort: "price", preferred_min_throughput: 40}` (tok/s; `preferred_max_latency` also exists) — because a pure price sort can route to a host queuing requests for minutes each. Add `require_parameters: true` when the call needs structured output (the cheapest host for a model does not always support it). Enable prompt caching when a large prefix is reused. Use `flex` tiers with OpenAi and Gemini that offer batch pricing at the cost of higher latency.
4. **Capture actual spend**: request usage/cost in the response and report it, so estimates can be checked against reality. If a run is substantially more expensive than estimated, stop and re-confirm.

# Coding practices

## Backward Compatibility and Tests

Only add backward-compatibility shims, fallbacks, or dual-format handling in production systems. During development, keep the code clean — delete the old format and move on. If unsure whether something needs backward compatibility, ask before adding it.

Ensure core functionality is covered by tests, but avoid slop and large sets of smoke tests. Less is more.

## Make Reruns Safe

For every command, lifecycle step, or processing loop that may be retried, restarted, or interrupted, design it to reach the correct end state after any number of runs. This includes file-writing scripts and batched external calls.

Check two cases: a second run after success, and a run after interruption at each step. If a prior run may have left partial or stale state, inspect it before continuing. Reuse completed work, repair incomplete outputs, and remove artifacts or locks only after confirming that they are stale.

When deciding whether work is complete, compare stable content or identifiers, not file count or creation order.

## Commands For Me To Run: Copy-Pasteable, Never Illustrative

Any command written for me to run should work as-is when pasted into my shell from the
project root. No placeholders I have to resolve, and no interpreter or tool that is
not on my PATH — I copy what you write and run it.

In practice this means naming the project's own interpreter or entry point rather than
a generic one: `.venv/bin/python -m extract.export --release abc123`, not
`python -m extract.export ...`.

## Verification Before Finishing

Always verify that changes work (run tests, render outputs, check results) before presenting them as complete. Don't leave the user with "to verify, do X" — do it yourself.

When modifying code that produces visual output (plots, charts, UI components), always render and visually inspect the result before presenting the change as complete. Never declare formatting fixes "done" based on code logic alone, except for internal-facing HTML pages. For these, trust your judgement.

When editing something that is deployed (e.g. a GH page), deploying it is part of the task. When the edit is trivial, deploy. When it needs my review, ask for confirmation - but never let me guess whether the latest update is live.

# Working with git

## Committing: Fetch Before Building a Commit Stack

`git fetch` and check `main...origin/main` BEFORE committing, especially when building a stack. 
Also check `git log` for local commits that appeared since the session started (a collaborator or another session may have committed from the same checkout); verify shared files weren't clobbered before stacking on top.

## Parallel Agents in Git Worktrees

- **Merge by the agent's merge-base, never against current main/master.** An agent branches from
  the state that existed when it started, so `git diff main <branch>` carries *deletions of
  everything merged since*; applying it silently reverts already-merged work, with nothing in the
  output to indicate it. Use
  `git diff $(git merge-base main <branch>) <branch> -- <file>` to get only the agent's own
  changes, and re-verify previously merged work after each merge — not just the piece just landed.
- **Remove each worktree as it lands, not at the end.** Each is a full checkout; a wide wave can
  fill the disk mid-session, and worktree creation then fails with "No space left on device".
</system-reminder>

Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type parameter to select which agent type to use. If omitted, the general-purpose agent is used.

## When to use

Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

absolute distance between the anchor and the true value (in cases where a true value existed)

divided by the true value such that a value of 1 indicated that the anchors were equal to the true

values and a value of 2 meant that anchors were on average 2 (or 1/2) times the true value.

estimated. In most studies, researchers simply ask participants whether the Eiffel tower is taller

and significance tests (Viechtbauer, 2010). Among continuous moderators (Table 2), only the

anchor distance had an effect on the anchoring effect size, which was positive. Among

categorical moderators (Table 3), type of anchor (no effects for subliminal or random anchors

and large effects for fixed and relevant anchors), type of task (e.g., largest effect for predicted

happiness, no effect for price estimates), comparative questions (small effect for paradigms

stimulus (no effect for audio/visual/image, large effect for brief written descriptions) affected

anchoring effect size.

size of anchoring effects, with more extreme anchors leading to larger effect sizes. The

proportion of female participants, the sample mean age, the publication year, and monetary

                                              Abstract

Anchoring effects are among the largest and easiest to replicate in social psychology. However,

the ship on which anchoring research is floating has become brittle with respect to three

domains: (a) the relationship between paradigm features (e.g., choice of anchor or type of scale)

and effect sizes is mostly unknown, (b) there are numerous contradictory findings on moderators

(e.g., role of incentives for accurate estimates), and (c) it is unclear which of the many theories

on anchoring effects is best supported by the evidence overall. Method: To increase clarity and

transparency in the field of anchoring effects research, we meta-analyzed the most

comprehensive collection of openly available anchoring effects data in existence today. Results:

We found large but also heterogeneous anchoring effects, g = 0.689, 95% CI [0.589, 0.789], σ² =

27:## 1. Anchoring: how the anchoring index changes with anchor spread (Open Anchoring Quest)
30:- **M1: resource-rational adjustment** (Lieder et al. 2018, https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8). A Metropolis–Hastings chain (a stepwise random-walk sampler) starts at the anchor and runs t steps of size s·σᵢ.
31:- **M2: Anchor Integration Model** (Turner & Schley 2016, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003). The estimate is a weighted mix of the anchor and a belief sample, with fixed weight w.
33:- **M4: plausibility-gated selective accessibility** (Mussweiler & Strack 1999, https://doi.org/10.1006/jesp.1998.1364; Wegener et al. 2001, https://doi.org/10.1006/jesp.2000.1431). An anchor loses its effect when it falls outside the plausible range.
36:- Fixed before OpAQ is loaded: s and t for M1, w for M2, k for M3. Each is calibrated to Jacowitz & Kahneman's (1995) anchoring index.
38:- Fitted per item on OpAQ: μᵢ, from `true_value` and the anchored data. σᵢ is taken from a proxy, the pooled within-condition SD. OpAQ has no unanchored SD per item, so the simulator computes the same proxy on its own simulated data, which keeps the comparison fair.
41:1. **Anchoring index (AI).** Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995 (https://doi.org/10.1177/01461672952111004) used anchors at the 15th and 85th percentiles and found a mean AI of 48.48%. Lieder's model gave 53.22% and an item-level correlation of r(13) = .62. These values are from the Lieder et al. preprint text. This is the calibration target. The test is the item-level correlation: it must be r ≥ .40.
42:2. **Anchor distance.** Anchoring grows with anchor distance: b = 0.040, k = 312, p < .001, "nonlinear but positive", with no inverted U (Röseler & Schütz 2022 meta-analysis of OpAQ, https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn; pooled g = 0.689 [0.589, 0.789]). A model must predict a positive slope of g on distance.
43:3. **Random anchors.** Explicitly random anchors have much smaller effects than fixed anchors (same source; also Schley & Weingarten 2026, https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.03238). M1 as published starts at any anchor and so predicts full-sized effects. **M1 fails this target unless the start point depends on how informative the anchor is. This is stated in advance.**
44:4. **Time pressure (contested).** M1 predicts more anchoring under time pressure. Lieder et al. (https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-017-1288-6) found that adjustment falls as time cost rises. Röseler et al. 2023 (https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/jztk2) did not find the time effect in 4 studies (N = 898). The paper must report this conflict alongside the new test.
46:**New prediction.** The measure is AI = (median log estimate under the high anchor − median under the low anchor) / (log a_H − log a_L), plotted against anchor spread (log a_H − log a_L) / σ̂ᵢ. The four models predict different shapes:
52:The existing evidence already goes against M3 and M4. The positive g–distance slope in target 2 contradicts M3, which predicts g flat once anchors pass the plausible range, and M4, which predicts g falling. So the open contrast is M1 against M2. Both predict a rising g, so g cannot separate them. The AI–spread slope can: it rises under M1 and stays flat under M2. M3 and M4 stay in the simulator as checks.
54:**Refutation rule.** Fit a multilevel regression of item AI on log spread, with random effects for study and a moderator for anchor type. A slope whose 95% CI lies entirely ≤ 0 refutes M1. A slope whose CI lies entirely > 0 refutes M2–M4. A CI that includes 0 with a half-width below 0.05 supports M2. The simulator converts these slopes into predicted intervals for each model before any data are loaded.
56:**Data.** Open Anchoring Quest, OSF https://osf.io/ygnvb/. Licence: **CC-BY 4.0** on the node that holds `OPAQ_JOPD.csv`; the components sz5b9, 4t5mu and gnr2x are also CC-BY 4.0. Contents: 96 studies, 21,359 participants, 412 items (355 with true values), 88,914 trials, an anchor-type code, and a high/low anchor flag (Röseler et al. 2022, https://doi.org/10.5334/jopd.67).
57:- **Optional site-level arm:** Many Labs 1 anchoring, OSF wx7ck, **CC0**. Site-level uncertainty should predict site-level anchoring. Reported anchoring SMDs are 1.21–2.53, τ .15–.69, I² 40–91% (Olsson-Collentine et al. 2020, https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000294, table read from postprint). OpAQ most likely already includes the Many Labs 1 anchoring data, so this arm tests a different prediction on overlapping data. It is not an independent replication.
68:- Most items have exactly two anchors, so the test works across items.
127:- **Field arm (extension, not part of the main test).** In GJP year 1, crowd-belief forecasters (conditions 2a–2c) were randomised against independent forecasters (1a–1c). They made about 1.3 forecasts per question (Mellers et al. 2014), so the crowd display mostly shaped the *first* forecast, and the revision rule has little to revise. This arm needs a different model, in which the displayed distribution acts as an anchor on the first forecast (close to M2 in design 1). Its targets would be spread per question-day and the difference in Brier score between conditions.
302:- **Design 1 item count.** The number of OpAQ items with large anchor spreads is unknown without reading the data. The preregistration needs a rule that declares the test uninformative if too few items qualify.
306:Scratch files (full texts, scripts, the anchoring simulation `scratch_mh_anchor.py`, and the DOI lists) are in `/tmp/jdmsim`, outside the project.

input.description: Schley/Weingarten + computational models
input.prompt:
You are doing part of a literature novelty check for a planned preregistered study. Return findings as your final message (no report files).

PLANNED STUDY (context): Using the Open Anchoring Quest (OpAQ) dataset (Röseler et al. 2022, J Open Psychol Data, doi 10.5334/jopd.67; 412 anchoring items, 96 studies), test how the PROPORTIONAL anchoring index (AI = (central estimate under high anchor − central estimate under low anchor) / (high anchor − low anchor); Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995) changes with anchor extremity (anchor distance relative to true value and/or to uncertainty about the quantity), at the item level, and compare against predictions simulated from four process models: resource-rational adjustment (Lieder et al. 2018 PBR), anchor integration model (Turner & Schley 2016 Cogn Psychol), insufficient adjustment (Epley & Gilovich 2006), selective accessibility / plausibility (Mussweiler & Strack; Wegener et al. 2001).

HARD CONSTRAINTS:
- Do NOT download or open any data file (csv, xlsx, rds, zip of data) from osf.io/ygnvb or any OSF data component, or any supplementary dataset. Papers (PDF/HTML text) only. This is a blinding rule.
- Write scratch files only as /tmp/jdmsim/scratch_nov_sw_* (unique prefix; other agents share that dir).
- Every number you report needs its source location (page, table, or section) in the text you read. Mark anything you only saw in an abstract as "abstract only" and anything not read as UNVERIFIED. Never fabricate DOIs; verify DOIs via https://api.crossref.org/works/<DOI>.
- OpenAlex: `set -a; source ~/.claude/api_keys.env; set +a`, then append `&api_key=<key>`; the default key is out of quota today, rotate through the comma-separated $OPENALEX_API_KEYS (a helper exists: `python3 /tmp/jdmsim/scratch_nov_oa.py search "<query>" "&filter=publication_year:2022-2026"` and `python3 /tmp/jdmsim/scratch_nov_oa.py cites <OpenAlexWorkID>`). Semantic Scholar API needs no key. Skills available: download-paper (download PDFs by DOI), check-claim. For PsyArXiv PDFs try the OSF API: https://api.osf.io/v2/preprints/<id>/?embed=primary_file then the file's download link (preprint PDFs are fine to download; data files are not).

TASKS:
A. Schley & Weingarten anchoring meta-analysis. Crossref shows: 10.31234/osf.io/teq7k (2023) and teq7k_v2 (2025-12) "50 Years of Anchoring Effects: A Theoretical Re-Integration and Meta-Analysis"; SSRN 10.2139/ssrn.4605057, 10.2139/ssrn.5893864, 10.2139/ssrn.5114456 ("50 Years of Anchoring: A Meta-Analysis and Meta-Study of Anchoring Effects"); and reportedly Management Science doi 10.1287/mnsc.2023.03238. Verify the MnSc DOI via Crossref (title, authors, year, volume/issue). Establish whether these are one paper or two. Read the FULL TEXT of the latest available version (prefer teq7k_v2 or the MnSc version). Extract precisely: (1) data sources (did they use OpAQ? how many effects/studies/items), (2) whether and how they coded anchor extremity/distance (definition: relative to true value? to uncertainty/SD? percentiles?), (3) at what level (effect/item/study) extremity moderation was tested and the exact numeric result, including any nonlinearity (inverted U?), (4) which effect-size metric(s) they used — Hedges g only, or any proportional/unitless adjustment metric such as the anchoring index, (5) which theories they contrasted and how (e.g., "meta-study", theory-driven predictions, model fitting?), (6) results for random/uninformative anchors. Quote key sentences with page numbers.
B. Young, Speekenbrink, Buyukyildirim, Chung et al. 2026, "Anchoring the anchor: judgments of both items assimilate in item-based anchoring", Cognitive Psychology, doi 10.1016/j.cogpsych.2026.101796. Read (full text if accessible, else abstract + any preprint). What did they do; did they use OpAQ data; did they fit computational models; any analysis of anchor extremity or proportional adjustment?
C. Search 2022–2026 for computational/process-model papers on numerical anchoring: queries like "anchoring computational model", "anchoring Bayesian model", "anchoring resource-rational", "anchoring sampling model estimation", "anchoring adjustment model fitting", "anchor extremity anchoring index", "anchoring index anchor distance", "anchor plausibility extremity nonmonotonic". Use OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, and WebSearch/Google Scholar-style searches (load WebSearch/WebFetch via ToolSearch "select:WebSearch,WebFetch"). Also check who cites Lieder et al. 2018 (10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8 and 10.3758/s13423-017-1288-6) and Turner & Schley 2016 (10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003) in 2022–2026 and flag any that fit models to multi-study/multi-item anchoring data or relate proportional adjustment to anchor extremity. For each relevant hit: citation, verified DOI, one-paragraph summary of design/measure/key numbers, and how close it is to the planned study (0–3).
D. Briefly: what exactly did Lieder et al. 2018 (both PBR papers) and Turner & Schley 2016 fit their models to (which datasets, how many items, which measures), and did either derive/test a prediction about how the anchoring index varies with anchor extremity? Give numbers (e.g., Lieder's simulated vs observed AI for Jacowitz & Kahneman items; any anchor-extremity simulations such as Russo & Schoemaker or Chapman & Johnson-type data). Page references.

Final message: structured findings per task A–D, with verified DOIs, page-referenced numbers, and a closeness rating to the planned study.

input.prompt:
You are doing part of a literature novelty check for a planned preregistered study. Return findings as your final message (no report files).

PLANNED STUDY (context): Using the Open Anchoring Quest dataset (412 anchoring items, 96 studies), test how the PROPORTIONAL anchoring index (AI = (central estimate under high anchor − central estimate under low anchor) / (high anchor − low anchor); Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995) changes with anchor extremity (distance relative to true value and/or to uncertainty about the quantity), at the item level, compared against simulated predictions of resource-rational adjustment (Lieder et al. 2018), anchor integration (Turner & Schley 2016), insufficient adjustment (Epley & Gilovich 2006), and selective accessibility / plausibility (Mussweiler & Strack; Wegener et al. 2001).

YOUR TASK: extract direct QUANTITATIVE evidence from primary texts on how anchoring (especially proportional adjustment / anchoring index, or anything convertible to it) varies with anchor extremity, including very extreme / implausible anchors. For each paper: full citation, DOI verified via https://api.crossref.org/works/<DOI> (title + first author must match), design (items, anchor levels and how extremity was defined), measure, and the exact numbers (means per anchor level, AI or % adjustment, whether the curve is linear, saturating, or inverted-U). Where the paper reports means and anchors but no AI, compute the implied AI yourself and show the arithmetic. Page/table references for every number.

Papers (priority order):
1. Chapman & Johnson 1994, "The limits of anchoring", J Behav Decis Mak (several anchor levels incl. extreme ones).
2. Strack & Mussweiler 1997 JPSP (plausible vs implausible/extreme anchors, e.g., Gandhi age, Einstein).
3. Mussweiler & Strack 2001 (implausible anchors / "considering the impossible"), and Mussweiler & Strack 2000 if relevant.
4. Wegener, Petty, Detweiler-Bedell & Jarvis 2001 JESP "Implications of attitude change theories for numerical anchoring: anchor plausibility and the limits of anchor effectiveness" (moderate vs extreme anchors × elaboration); Wegener et al. 2010 (Advances in Exp Soc Psych chapter on elaboration and anchoring) if it reports numbers.
5. Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995 PSPB: AI with 15th/85th percentile anchors, per-item values if given, asymmetry high vs low.
6. Thorsteinson 2011 (anchor extremity in performance ratings, J Appl Soc Psychol?), Hardt/others with inverted-U ("Anchor extremity" literature).
7. Simmons, LeBoeuf & Nelson 2010 JPSP (uncertainty about direction; adjustment).
8. Frederick & Mochon 2012 JEP:General "A scale distortion theory of anchoring".
9. Schultze, Rakotoarisoa & Schulz-Hardt 2015 (distance between initial estimate and advice — shape of the adjustment vs distance curve; they are cited as a model for formalising distance vs adjustment).
10. Townson 2019 (anchoring; check what it is — possibly a thesis or paper on anchor extremity).
11. Bystranowski et al. 2021 meta-analysis of anchoring in legal judgments (did they test anchor extremity? result).
12. Harris et al. 2019 and Shanks et al. 2020 (incentives / replication of anchoring; any AI values), Bahník & Strack (any extremity work).
13. Any other study you find with ≥3 anchor levels on the same items reporting estimates per level (e.g., Russo & Schoemaker; Mussweiler 2001 "the durability of anchoring"; Hardt & Pohl; Smith & Windschitl; Critcher & Gilovich; LeBoeuf & Shafir 2006 "the long and short of it" — proportional adjustment in physical anchoring).

HARD CONSTRAINTS:
- Do NOT download or open any data file (csv, xlsx, sav, rds, data zips) from OSF or any repository, especially the Open Anchoring Quest (osf.io/ygnvb) — this is a blinding rule. Papers (PDF/HTML text) only.
- Write scratch files only as /tmp/jdmsim/scratch_nov_classic_* (unique prefix; other agents share that dir).
- Use the download-paper skill to obtain PDFs by DOI (it uses open-access routes and the user's signed-in Chrome for paywalled sources); check-claim skill is also available. If you cannot obtain a full text, say so and mark numbers from secondary sources as SECONDARY (name the source) or UNVERIFIED. Never fabricate DOIs or numbers.
- OpenAlex (if needed): `set -a; source ~/.claude/api_keys.env; set +a`; the default key is out of quota today, rotate through comma-separated $OPENALEX_API_KEYS; helper: `python3 /tmp/jdmsim/scratch_nov_oa.py search "<query>"`.

Final message: a per-paper list with verified citation+DOI, design, numbers (with page refs), implied AI where computable, and one line on what it implies for how AI varies with extremity. End with a short synthesis: what quantitative predictions exist in the literature for AI vs extremity, and which gaps remain.

ANCHORING EFFECTS META-ANALYSIS                                                                1



                                              Abstract

Anchoring effects are among the largest and easiest to replicate in social psychology. However,

the ship on which anchoring research is floating has become brittle with respect to three

domains: (a) the relationship between paradigm features (e.g., choice of anchor or type of scale)

and effect sizes is mostly unknown, (b) there are numerous contradictory findings on moderators

(e.g., role of incentives for accurate estimates), and (c) it is unclear which of the many theories

on anchoring effects is best supported by the evidence overall. Method: To increase clarity and

transparency in the field of anchoring effects research, we meta-analyzed the most

comprehensive collection of openly available anchoring effects data in existence today. Results:

We found large but also heterogeneous anchoring effects, g = 0.689, 95% CI [0.589, 0.789], σ² =

0.21, Ntotal = 17,708, k = 393. (a) Anchors communicated as randomly determined did not have

effects, and some effects reversed when visual response scales were used. (b) For many

previously contradictory results, we found null effects (e.g., incentives did not affect the

magnitude of anchoring effects). (c) Overall, theories of anchoring that stress rationality and

nonlinearity were best supported by the results. Discussion: By applying an open and robust

empirical procedure, we provide anchoring researchers with a new ship. We recommend that

future research increase trust in findings through preregistration, reduce heterogeneity between

anchoring effects through standardization, and better explain the impact of moderators. Data and

analyses are available online

(https://osf.io/4t5mu/?view_only=60c4d81cd5044a2899482c6eb92fee32).

       Keywords: anchoring effect meta-analysis, open science, open data
 ANCHORING EFFECTS META-ANALYSIS                                                               2



      Providing the Anchor With a New Ship: A Meta-Analysis of Anchoring Effects
       Trivial everyday judgments (e.g., the number of calories in one’s lunch) but also serious

ones (e.g., the length of a prison sentence) require people to make numeric estimates. When

people consider a number prior to making such an estimate, they will likely be biased toward that

number. Such anchoring effects have most prominently been described by Kahneman and

Tversky (1974) and are similar to other biases, such as hindsight bias (Pohl et al., 2003),

including useless advice in one’s decisions (Schultze et al., 2017; Teovanović et al., 2015), or

confirmation bias (Mussweiler & Strack, 1999b). Anchoring effects are among the most robust

phenomena in social psychology (Kahneman, 2012, p. 119), and they have been found in many

different paradigms.

before a valid theory can be developed, three problems need to be solved. So far: (a) Paradigms

SUSCEPTILITY TO ANCHORING EFFECTS




                        Testing the Reliability of Anchoring Susceptibility Scores

                                      Lucia Weber1 and Lukas Röseler2




       1
           Faculty of Medicine, University of Zurich, Switzerland

       2
           Münster Center for Open Science, University of Münster, Germany




                                                Author Note

       Lucia Weber

       Lukas Röseler       https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6446-1901

       Correspondence concerning this article should be addressed to Lukas Röseler, University

of Münster. Email: [email redacted]




                                             Preprint Version

       This manuscript corresponds to the corrected version of the article published in EJOP

(February 2025). This manuscript has not been peer reviewed in this form.
 SUSCEPTIBILITY TO ANCHORING EFFECTS


                                                Abstract

Whereas anchoring is a very robust and well-known effect that refers to the assimilation of

numeric estimates toward previously considered numbers, the psychological mechanisms

behind it have yet to be fully clarified. Research on theories on how susceptibility to

anchoring is related to other personality parameters has not been able to provide sufficient

empirical evidence of such relationships. A probable explanation is that anchoring scores lack

reliability in most anchoring experiments. The present research examined whether reliability

depends on the type of score used to capture anchoring susceptibility. In a classical anchoring

experiment, men and women aged between 14 and 67 years (N = 78) were asked to estimate

the true values of certain numbers (e.g., height of the Zugspitze mountain) after being

confronted with either a high or a low anchor number. Four different anchoring scores that are

commonly used to measure susceptibility to anchoring in anchoring research were computed

for every person, as well as the scores’ reliabilities. The number and types of items were

chosen to allow for reliable and valid measurement. Anchoring effects were present, but the

reliabilities of all four scores were either very low or zero. These results reinforce the

reliability problem that was also described by previous research. So far, there are no

conditions under which anchoring susceptibility can be measured reliably, suggesting the

development of new measures or even questioning the existence of individual differences in

susceptibility to anchoring. In further research, other person-independent factors that may

influence anchoring strength should be investigated to develop theories that can explain the

psychological mechanisms behind anchoring.

Keywords: anchoring, anchoring effect, anchoring scores, anchoring strength, reliability
 SUSCEPTIBILITY TO ANCHORING EFFECTS

Anchoring describes the phenomenon that people are influenced by a previously considered

number when making a numerical estimate. In studies on the anchoring effect, people are

initially confronted with an anchor number—often by having to respond to a comparative

question, such as “Is the height of Mount Everest larger or smaller than 5,000 meters?” After

answering this first question, when asked to give an actual estimate, people tend to assimilate

their answer toward the anchor.

         It has been proposed that people differ in the extent to which they are susceptible to

this effect, depending on certain individual differences, such as general knowledge, cognitive

abilities (e.g., Bergman et al., 2010), or the Big Five (e.g., McElroy & Dowd, 2007). The

implicit assumption that susceptibility to anchoring is a person parameter can be found at the

core of anchoring models, which aim to clarify which psychological mechanisms underlie

anchoring effects, for example, in the Insufficient Adjustment Model (Epley & Gilovich,

2001).

         In order to confirm and expand on these theories, considerable research effort has been

put toward finding evidence for the moderating effects of personality traits on anchoring

susceptibility—resulting in very mixed findings. Although significant effects have been found

in many cases (Bergman et al., 2010; Cheek & Norem, 2022; Epley & Gilovich, 2006; Eroglu

& Croxton, 2010; McElroy & Dowd, 2007; Teovanović, 2019), replication attempts have

often failed (Cheek & Norem, 2019; Furnham et al., 2012; Stanovich & West, 2008) and

meta-analyses have shown that for numerous moderators of personality, the average effect

sizes are indistinguishable from zero (Röseler, 2021).

         A probable reason for this pattern of results is that anchoring susceptibility has not

been measured reliably in these studies, making it impossible to find significant correlations

with other constructs. This reliability problem as an explanation for unclear findings was first

described by Röseler, Schütz, and Starker (2019) and was then further explained and backed
 SUSCEPTIBILITY TO ANCHORING EFFECTS

up by an extensive amount of evidence, showing very low reliabilities for measures of

anchoring susceptibility in a large proportion of personality moderator research on anchoring

(Röseler, 2021; Schindler et al., 2021). These findings raise questions about the conditions

under which anchoring susceptibility can be measured reliably or whether it cannot be

measured reliably at all.

al., 2023) was created. In this project, data from as many existing anchoring experiments as
possible are being meta-analytically aggregated into one large data set. The methodology in
the included studies varies to a great extent, such as in how the anchoring task is
implemented, or in other parameters, such as sample size. The OpAQ data set makes it
possible to systematically investigate the influence of a range of these factors on the reliability
of anchoring susceptibility measurements.
        One factor that has varied across studies is how the score depicting susceptibility to
anchoring was calculated. Whereas the basis for this score is the difference between the true
value of the item and the anchor value in all cases, there are various ways in which this
difference has been converted into a score. These differences could be crucial for explaining
different outcomes in the reliability. As the structure of the OpAQ data set is trial-based, it
provides the opportunity to calculate the different anchoring susceptibility scores by using
data from all the studies included in the data set. So far, evaluations have indicated that
different ways of computing anchoring susceptibility actually lead to scores with different
reliabilities.
        In the present research, we examined this assumption in a classical anchoring
experiment where people make estimates about certain measurements (e.g., the height of a
mountain) after being confronted with either a high or a low anchor. Most studies in the
OpAQ data set have used a small number of items, which makes it difficult to have reliable
 SUSCEPTIBILITY TO ANCHORING EFFECTS
anchoring scores. These items are also oftentimes very homogeneous (e.g., only estimates of
the lengths of rivers), so the validity of anchoring susceptibility is also questionable, as it can
be confounded with a person’s ability to give correct estimates in a certain area of knowledge.
To allow for reliable and valid measurements of anchoring susceptibility in the present
research, we used a large number of heterogeneous items, which varied in the size of their
true values, the unit of measurement, and area of knowledge.

import json, sys, urllib.request, urllib.parse
refs = [l.strip() for l in open(sys.argv[1]) if l.strip()]
for r in refs:
    url = "https://api.crossref.org/works?rows=2&mailto=[email redacted]&query.bibliographic=" + urllib.parse.quote(r)
    try:
        d = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=30))
    except Exception as e:
        print("ERR", r, e); continue
    print("### ", r)
    for it in d["message"]["items"]:
        au = it.get("author", [{}])
        a1 = au[0].get("family", "?") if au else "?"
        yr = (it.get("issued", {}).get("date-parts", [[None]])[0][0])
        print("   ", it["DOI"], "|", a1, yr, "|", (it.get("title") or ["?"])[0][:110], "|", (it.get("container-title") or ["?"])[0][:50])

"""Verify DOIs against Crossref. Input file: one line per DOI as  DOI|expected first-author family name|title fragment
Prints MATCH/MISMATCH with the Crossref record (first author, year, title, journal, vol/issue/pages)."""
import json, sys, urllib.request, unicodedata
def norm(s): return unicodedata.normalize('NFKD', s or '').encode('ascii', 'ignore').decode().lower()
for line in open(sys.argv[1]):
    if not line.strip() or line.startswith('#'): continue
    doi, fam, frag = [x.strip() for x in line.split('|')]
    try:
        m = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(f"https://api.crossref.org/works/{doi}?mailto=[email redacted]", timeout=30))['message']
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"ERROR   {doi}: {e}"); continue
    au = m.get('author') or [{}]
    a1 = au[0].get('family') or au[0].get('name', '?')
    title = (m.get('title') or ['?'])[0]
    yr = (m.get('issued', {}).get('date-parts') or [[None]])[0][0]
    ok = norm(fam) in norm(a1) and norm(frag) in norm(title)
    print(f"{'MATCH   ' if ok else 'MISMATCH'} {doi} | {a1} {yr} | {title} | {(m.get('container-title') or ['-'])[0]} {m.get('volume','')}({m.get('issue','')}) {m.get('page','')} | n_authors={len(au)}")
EOF

the relationship between anchor extremeness and effect size: Chapman and Johnson (1994)
reported a nonlinear relationship, but they used the geometric (instead of the more widely used
arithmetic) mean of estimates, but using the geometric mean would result in a nonlinear

analyses (Bystranowski et al., 2021; Townson, 2019) have suggested that there may even be an
inverted u-shaped relationship.

Anchor Extremeness
       Another area where anchoring theories have diverged to some extent involves the
question of whether more extreme anchors lead to larger anchoring effects. For example, a
researcher can choose a question for which the true value is 42 and use an anchor that is not
extreme, such as 50, but also an extreme anchor, such as 500. According to the Insufficient
Adjustment Model, people adjust until they arrive at their range of plausible values (Epley &
Gilovich, 2004). For example, if plausible values for the length of a sentence range from 2 to 30

       To account for interactions of moderators not considered above, we conducted a
classification and regression tree analysis using the random-effects Meta-CART model (Breiman
et al., 1998) and the corresponding R packages (X. Li et al., 2020). Classification trees are
designed to detect interactions that can be interpreted easily. The models can handle nonlinearity,
work with categorical and continuous variables, and work fully automatically. Meta-CART
divides the entire sample of effect sizes into groups with the aim of minimizing within-group
heterogeneity. This step is repeated until the exit criteria are met (e.g., the number of effect sizes

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

/confirmatory-analyses-first/value/first/value/question1c/value : ASYMMETRY HYPOTHESIS

Pair 1 (there should be no significant difference in the means of these variables if the ADM is correct)
- STA-ADM-Score based on one pair of ADM-anchors (true value: 45) for high anchors
- STA-ADM-Score based on one pair of ADM-anchors (true value: 45) for low anchors

Pair 2 (there should be no significant difference in the means of these variables if the RDM is correct)
- STA-RDM-Score based on one pair of RDM-anchors (true value: 45) for high anchors
- STA-RDM-Score based on one pair of RDM-anchors (true value: 45) for low anchors

STA-Scores are calculated as an index of difference between unanchored estimates and anchored estimates:
- Absolute Difference Model: Anchored estimates are assumed to be the weighted arithmetic mean of unanchored estimates and the anchor. For one case, the STA-Score is the weight of the anchor. 1-STA(adm) is the weight of the unanchored estimate. The sum of weights must be 1.
- Relative Differences Model: Anchored estimates are assumed to be the weighted geometric mean of unanchored estimates and the anchor. For one case, the STA-Score is the weight of the anchor. 2-STA(rdm) is the weight of the unanchored estimate. The sum of weights must be 2.
/confirmatory-analyses-first/value/first/value/question2c/value : Multilevel Model and planned t-tests for pairwise comparisons
/confirmatory-analyses-first/value/first/value/question3c/value : The 4 variables follow a 2x2 design:
- high versus low anchor
- ADM versus RDM STA-Score
/confirmatory-analyses-third/value/third/value/question1c/value : Individual Differences Hypothesis A: Test if ADM and RDM STA-Scores are different.
ADM-STA-Scores and RDM-STA-Scores will be computed via the following R-Code (w1):

function(estimate_unanchored, estimate_anchored, anchor, model = "adm") {
  
  if (model == "adm") {
    w1 <- (estimate_anchored - estimate_unanchored)/(anchor - estimate_unanchored)
    w2 <- 1-w1
    
    return(w1)
    
  } else if (model == "rdm") {
    rdm_pred <- function(estimate_unanchored, anchor, weight) {
      e_pred <- sqrt(estimate_unanchored^(2-weight)*anchor^weight)  # computes the weighted geometric mean of estimate and anchor
      return(e_pred)
    }
    
    
    f <- function(x) {
      abs(rdm_pred(estimate_unanchored = estimate_unanchored
                   , anchor = anchor
                   , weight = x) - estimate_anchored)
    }
    
    optimize <- (optimize(f, lower = -50, upper = 50, maximum = FALSE))$minimum
    w1 <- optimize
    w2 <- 2-w1
    
    return(w1)
    
    
  } else {
    return("Model must be adm or rdm.")
  }
}

Absolute Adjustment = abs(anchored estimate - anchor)
We will compute the absolute adjustment from anchors (smaller values correspond to a higher susceptibility to anchoring effects) for all 32 estimates per participant.

Logarithmized Absolute Adjustment (Log Adjustment) = log(Absolute Adjustment)
Note: For cases which had the anchor "0", we will also use the log-Anchor "0" because log(0) is undefined. 
Note: All logs are for the base of e = 2.718282 (in R: exp(1)).

Exclusions:
- Due to no possibility to compute logarithms of negative values, we will only consider adjustments from high anchors for this hypothesis.

2. We will compare the correlations.
If rADM >= rRDM: ADM is sufficient.
If rADM < rRDM: RDM is more accurate.

                             Judgment and Decision Making, Vol. 16, No. 1, January 2021, pp. 131–141




                                                     Anchoring without scale distortion

                                                                                       Štěpán Bahník∗



                                                                                               Abstract

                                          The scale distortion theory of anchoring argues that people are inﬂuenced by a
                                      previously considered numeric value, an anchor, because the anchor distorts the scale
                                      on which a subsequent judgment is made. The distortion of the scale due to the anchor
                                      is a momentary eﬀect that would be overridden if the scale was distorted again, for
                                      example, by consideration of a diﬀerent value on the same scale. In the present study,
                                      participants compared thirteen random anchors on the same scale to thirteen diﬀerent
                                      objects. Subsequent numeric estimates of objects’ attributes were inﬂuenced by the
                                      corresponding anchors even though the anchors were divided from the estimates by
