Judgment and Decision Making (2023), Vol. 18:e34 1–23
doi:10.1017/jdm.2023.31
EMPIRICAL ARTICLE
Connecting the dots: Nonlinear patterns in the presence
of symbolic and nonsymbolic numerical standards
Roland Imhoff           1,2 and Paul Barker1
1 Social Cognition Center Cologne, University of Cologne, Cologne, Germany and 2 Social and Legal Psychology, Johannes
Gutenberg University Mainz, Mainz, Germany
Corresponding author: Roland Imhoff; Email: [email redacted]
Received: 9 March 2023; Revised: 23 May 2023; Accepted: 17 July 2023
Keywords: anchoring; contrast; enumeration; numerical representations
Abstract
Much like other social and nonsocial evaluations, estimates of numerical quantities are susceptible to comparative
inﬂuences. However, numerical representations can take either a nonsymbolic (e.g., a grouping of dots) or a
symbolic numerical form (e.g., Hindu–Arabic numerals), which each produce comparative biases in opposite
directions. The current work takes a ﬁne-grained curve ﬁtting approach across a wide range of values to the
investigation of their potential nonlinear inﬂuence in the context of a numerical estimation task. A series of 3
experiments (N = 1,613) showed how nonsymbolic standards produce linear contrastive patterns (Study 1), whereas
symbolic numerical anchors show a cubic assimilative effect with a leveling off in strength for more extreme
standards (Study 2). Sequential contrast from the previous patterns and assimilation to the previous response were
found to be present and additive in the presence of both representations but were larger in absence of the symbolic
numerical anchors (Study 3).
1. Introduction
Imagine, you have the task to estimate the number of political supporters at the presidential inauguration
ceremony of Donald Trump. As virtually any judgment, your exact estimate will be susceptible to
potentially irrelevant inﬂuences such as a more or less arbitrarily chosen comparison standards (e.g.,
supporters on Barack Obama’s 2009 inauguration). Importantly, this standard could be presented
as a merely numerical symbolic representation (i.e., the number 1.8 million) or non-symbolically
as a pictorial representation of the crowd. While the former has been well-established to prompt
assimilative anchoring effects (the judgment moves closer to the 1.8 million), the latter is more likely
to produce contrast (Trump’s crowd looks small when compared visually). The present research sought
to revisit these different comparative effects in light of recent developments in social comparison
research highlighting the importance of nonlinear relationship (Barker and Imhoff, 2021). For social
judgments, the strength of assimilation decreases with increased extremity of a comparison standard,
ultimately leading to contrast effects, a data pattern that can be modeled by a positive linear in
combination with a negative cubic effect (Barker and Imhoff, 2021). Although it is still unclear if
such nonlinearity extends to these more basic comparative judgments, theoretical accounts predict both
the contrastive effects, reported for nonsymbolic numerical representations, as well as the anchoring
© The Author(s), 2023. Published by Cambridge University Press on behalf of European Association of Decision Making and Society for
Judgment and Decision Making. This is an Open Access article, distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution licence
(https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0), which permits unrestricted re-use, distribution and reproduction, provided the original article is
properly cited.
            2       Roland Imhoff and Paul Barker
effects, for symbolic numerical representations, to produce these complex patterns. The current work
will investigate these possibilities for both of these representations of numerical standards as well as
their sequential dependencies on previous responses and standards, offering additional insights into the
various processes that underlie both phenomena.
To facilitate the ﬂow of our argument, let us provide an illustrative example. Imagine a situation
of a protest and a counter-protest (not an infrequent occurrence in most European cities). As a police
ofﬁcer, your task is to estimate the number of protestors in order to allocate a proportional number of
accompanying police forces. The comparative question underlying our research is now: How will the
size of the counter protest and the modality of receiving this information affect your estimate? Will the
number of protestors seem larger next to a small counter-protest and smaller next to a huge one? Will
it make a difference if you see the 2 protests as clusters of people or whether a colleague provides you
with the number of counter-protestors in a numerical, symbolic way?
Many of our perceptions and judgments rely heavily on the context surrounding the stimuli we
are about to judge. In the famous Ebbinghaus illusion, for instance, the central circle is consistently
overestimated or underestimated based on whether the circles surrounding it are smaller or larger.

state, have been found in both simultaneous and sequential magnitude judgments across various

an additive way (Mochon and Frederick, 2013). Finally, the study also probed if the sequential contrast
from previous standards still occurred when concrete symbolic numerical representations are available
within each the trial. In other words, the study was designed to provide insight whether a clear numeric
anchor will overrule the inﬂuence of the previous trial.
3.1. Method
3.1.1. Participants
The number of participants for this study was increased as a shortened online format was implemented.
The necessary sample size of 800 participants was again determined using simulations based on the
effect sizes and parameters found in previous work in the social comparative domain that used a similar
paradigm (Barker and Imhoff, 2021). Therefore, 803 participants recruited via Proliﬁc Academic
completed the study for a reward of £1.25. This ﬁnal sample consisted of 59% females and was aged
between 18 and 74 years (M = 35.48, SD = 13.31).
3.1.2. DJT-41
As in the previous experiment, each trial consisted of a target image (indicated by “judgment target”)
for which the number of dots had to be estimated horizontally next to a standard image (both images
300 × 300 pixel) without any time constraints. For half of the trials, the target image was on the left and
the standard on the right, for the other half it was vice versa. In order to rule out confusion regarding
which image to estimate, participants had to click a radio button to indicate what they thought the target
image was (trials with wrong clicks were excluded). Different from the previous study, the nonsymbolic
dot pattern of the standard was now accompanied by the symbolic numeric information displaying the
actual number of dots presented in this standard (“This image contains [between 93 and 901] dots.”).
A visual display of the trials can be found on OSF.
For better use online and to reduce strain on participants, the DJT was shortened to include just
41 trials per participant. In order to keep a similar granularity in measurement steps, however, 2
counterbalancing conditions were created so that half of the participants were randomly assigned to
either estimate 41 dot patterns of around 500 dots (±10 dots) next to standards that varied between
400 dots above or below the target image in intervals of 20 dots. The second group judged 40 similar
dot images in the presence of standards at each 20-dot-interval between 390 dots below or above
the target image as well as one in which the both images had an equal number of dots. In effect,
this counterbalancing offers the same 81-step precision in measurement that was also included in the
previous study.
3.1.3. Additional measures
Again, some basic demographics were recorded, including age, sex, and education, although the
INCOM was no longer administered in this study. An additional item was included at the start of the
survey to check for correct image display by asking participants to describe what they saw on a simple
image containing 3 shapes of different colors. A small traditional anchoring task, closely modeled on
the task and one of the questions in Strack and Mussweiler’s work (1997), was also included after the
main task for exploratory purposes not directly related to this line of research. This task and its analysis
are described in detail in the additional materials available online. After this, an open-ended item
was included to gauge participant’s suspicions regarding the goal of the current study. Finally, a new
            10        Roland Imhoff and Paul Barker
data-quality item was included in which participants were asked to indicate if their responses were
made in earnest or not in order to increase the quality of the data in the ﬁnal analyses. Participants were
guaranteed to not be affected in any way based on their responses to this item, but that it would help the
researchers in their investigation if they responded honestly. Responses were given on a Likert scale
ranging from “Deﬁnitely do not use my data” (1) to “Deﬁnitely use my data” (4). Responses of 2 or
lower were taken as an indication of poor data-quality and used for the exclusion of participants from
the analyses.
3.1.4. Procedure
Participants were fully informed about the data storage policy, procedure, and their rights before they
were asked for their consent to take part in the study. After the image display check and demographics
items participants completed 2 practice trails to get familiarized with the procedure of the main task.
Randomly allocated to 1 of the 2 counter balancing conditions, participants completed the main batch of
41 trials and afterward the traditional anchoring task. After this, the suspicion check item and the data-
quality item were presented before participants were debriefed, thanked and given their compensation.
The study lasted about 10 min.
3.1.5. Data treatment
Nonnumeric and empty responses made up 1% of trials while 0.7% showed a failed attention check
leading to their exclusion. This time, responses that exceeded the maximum or minimum standard
value (lower than 100 or higher than 900) were also removed (0.5%) to increase data quality, as such
estimates are unlikely to be honest estimates as a clear reference was available. The remaining scores
were z-transformed separately per participant to account for personal differences in response ranges.
Z-scores above 3 or below −3, or instances where no z-score could be calculated were removed (e.g.,
because participants always gave the same estimate, resulting in a denominator of zero), which was the
case for 0.2% of trials. Due to co-occurrences of these criteria a total of 2.4% of the original trials were
not used in the analyses. In addition, 12 participants indicated their data quality was low and should not
be included in the analysis. Combined the exclusion criteria left a total of 790 participants with data
suitable for use in the main analysis.
3.2. Results
Again, the main analysis took the form of a mixed model regression with REML that included ﬁxed
effects for the number of dots present in the target, as well as the standard (and additionally given as
a numeric anchor below the standard) in hundreds and modeled up to the third polynomials term. We
included random slopes of the 3 polynomials as well as the actual number of dots for participants to
account for participant level variation in patterns (no random intercept was estimated due to singular
ﬁt issues). As in Study 1, participants were above-chance accurate in detecting subtle differences in the

theses association became purely assimilative in nature. Furthermore, the association took on a slightly

The pattern of a positive linear and a negative cubic relation mimics recent ﬁndings in the ﬁeld
of social comparisons, with the exception that in the current studies very extreme standards do not
produce manifest contrast (Barker and Imhoff, 2021). These ﬁndings are compatible with previous
work describing the effects of extreme anchors (Chapman and Johnson, 1994; Mussweiler and Strack,
2001), and predictions based on insufﬁcient adjustment accounts (Tversky and Kahneman, 1974).
People form an impression of a plausible range of estimates and correct either upward or downward
from the given numerical anchor. They stop this correction as soon as the range of plausible estimates
is entered. More extreme anchors will then only result in an extended adjustment, not in a shifted range
of plausible estimates. An alternative explanation might be that extreme numerical symbolic values
bear less informative weight; and thus, the contrasting force of the nonsymbolic representation wins
through. Future research presenting either symbolic and nonsymbolic (as in the current study) or only
symbolic information can test these 2 explanations.
Additionally, the insufﬁcient adjustment accounts, in which respondents stop adjusting at the
boundary of the range of plausible values, do not offer a suitable explanations for the additive sequential
anchoring effects that were also found. The scale distortion account, on the other hand, does predict an
additive anchoring effect based on the fact that the contrast effects that are ultimately responsible for
the distortion of the response scale and eventual assimilative effects themselves work in an additive
way (Mochon and Frederick, 2013). In this way, the additive sequential anchoring effects, which can
work both to strengthen and to dampen the simultaneous anchoring effect can be explained by a single
mechanism.

content.content:
Study 2b
       In addition to the main DJT part of Study 2, a traditional anchoring paradigm was
included at the end of the work. The same participant, therefore, completed this study.
Method
       Task. Near the end of Study 2, the 803 participants from Study 02 were asked
whether the Cologne cathedral was higher or lower than some random anchor ranging from
10 to 390 meters in 20 meter intervals. Respondents then indicated whether they thought it
was higher or lower than this amount by using a radio button. As a follow up question
respondents were then asked to give their exact estimate for the height of the cathedral in
meters. These scores and the anchor values were then centred on the true size of the cathedral
(157 meters) so that score indicate the number of meters the response or anchor is removed
from the true answer.
       Data treatment. Twelve respondents indicated their data were of low quality and
were removed along with 16 non-numeric responses. Finally, one further scores above or
below 3 standard deviations from the average remaining responses were removed leaving 774
responses in total.
Results
       Orthogonal polynomials for the centred anchors up to the third term were regressed
on the centred scores, indicating a simple positive linear model best fit the data, t(770) =
8.96, β = 2009.54, 95% CI[1569.19, 2449.89], p < .001, with all other polynomial terms p >
.63. To give a more precise interpretation of the anchoring pattern, the simple linear model
was refit in isolation uncovering a clear assimilative pattern where each meter increase in the
anchor produced a 0.62meter increase in the response, t(772) = 8.97, β = 0.62, 95% CI[0.49,
0.76], p < .001, (Figure S1).
 Figure S1. Predicted responses in meters for each anchor step and predicted 95%CI.
Discussion
         In contrast to the findings in the main part of Study 02, the classical anchoring
paradigm did not show the expected levelling off of the anchoring effect even for the most
extreme anchors of 10 or 390 meters. The upward bound of which is more than twice as large
as the true value of the Cologne Cathedral (157 meters) and 10 meters taller than the Empire
State Building. It may still be that, due to the poor knowledge participants had of the
cathedral or other buildings, the anchors were not yet extreme enough to fall outside the
range of plausible values held by participants. Nevertheless, the findings here do not support
an insufficient adjustment account of anchoring and do not reproduce the findings on extreme
standards within a more classic anchoring paradigm that does not include sequential effects.

# Article Summary

**Title:** Falsifying the Insufficient Adjustment Model: No Evidence for Unidirectional Adjustment From Anchors

**Authors:** Lukas Röseler, Lisa Incerti, Tobias R. Rebholz, Christian Seida, Frank Papenmeier

**Year:** 2025

**DOI:** https://doi.org/10.15626/MP.2024.4137

**Abstract:**
The study examines whether time pressure intensifies anchoring effects through incomplete adjustment. Across four studies (N=898), researchers found no support for this hypothesis. Notably, anchoring effects disappeared when researchers employed alternative methodologies—visual scales or two-alternative forced-choice tasks—instead of traditional paradigms. While the authors conclude "the current version of the insufficient adjustment model should be discarded," they maintain that adjustment-based frameworks remain promising for future anchoring research, offering recommendations for refinement.

**Focus Area:** This research concerns **relative adjustment**—specifically investigating whether time constraints reduce how far participants adjust their estimates away from anchor values, testing a core mechanism of adjustment theory.

# Abstract and Full-Text Link

## Abstract
The research investigates anchoring effects—"the attraction of numerical judgments toward a previously considered number"—and their personality moderators. Meta-analyses of eight personality traits (Big Five, cognitive ability, cognitive reflection, self-control) found "no evidence of any personality moderator of anchoring." The author suggests measurement reliability issues may explain these null results.

## Full-Text PDF Link
- **Bitstream URL:** https://fis.uni-bamberg.de/bitstreams/6b8bc0b9-31e8-41e1-a052-4982dc18ea66/download

## Mention of Specific Concepts
The abstract does **not** mention absolute versus relative adjustment, geometric mean, or anchor distance/extremeness. It references "the anchoring and adjustment model" as a potential source for deriving parameters, but provides no details on these specific mechanisms.

       3.4.1. Computation of Susceptibility to Anchoring
       There are many ways to compute an individual’s susceptibility to anchoring. For
example, one can simply use the estimate for a given question and anchor, or compute the
relative absolute adjustment, that is, the absolute difference between the anchor and the estimate
divided by the true value (if a true value for the question exists) or an unanchored estimate (if an
unanchored for the question exists). In some cases, authors used the difference between anchor
and estimate. Cheek and Norem (2018, p. 2) argue that the use of differences between anchors
and estimates is an inappropriate measure of susceptibility to anchoring. They recommend using
absolute differences, instead. Röseler et al. (2019, p. 14) followed the recommendation and did
not find it to alter the correlation between cognitive ability and the susceptibility to anchoring.
       In paradigms with within-subjects manipulation of the anchors (i.e., the correct value is
the same for two items but the anchors are above and below the value; e.g., Röseler, Schütz,
Dolling et al., 2020) one can also compute the difference between the two respective estimates to
                                                                                                   39
measure the susceptibility to anchoring. However, the use of difference scores is often (and
necessarily) associated with low reliability regardless of the construct under investigation (Peter
et al., 1993). Röseler, Schütz, Dolling et al. (2020, Table 2) compared the reliabilities of absolute
adjustment scores with difference scores and found no differences in the inter-item correlations,
r(121) = .052, and r(121) = -.086, respectively.
       Another area of research that is underrated for the computation of anchoring scores is
research on the association between anchor extremeness and anchoring effect strength. The
knowledge that doubling the anchor’s distance from the true value does not double the effect size
(Chapman & Johnson, 1994; Thorsteinson, 2011; Wegener et al., 2001) has not yet been
integrated in the computation of anchoring scores. Moreover, there is no consensus with regards
to the focal elements of the anchoring paradigm such as (a) reference point and (b) distances of
anchors. (a) For example, if people have to estimate the number of words in this section, the
reference value can be the true number but also the unanchored estimate of the same or another
sample. (b) In studies where multiple items have the same true value and anchors are
manipulated, it is unclear whether they should be symmetrical or asymmetrical and whether they
should be absolute values such as ±50 units (e.g., Röseler et al., 2019) on the respective scale or
relative values such as ±50% (e.g., Teovanović, 2019). Ideally, researchers should know the
relationship between the size of the anchor and anchor effect strength, include a parameter for
the individual and compute the individual susceptibility to anchoring based on that relationship.
However, such an approach does not yet exist.

(Röseler et al., 2019, pp. 13-14) and 14 of them were experimenter provided. I computed the
relative distance between the high and low anchors and the true value for each item (i.e., anchor
minus true value divided by anchor), which was between .13 (age estimate for 53 years old
celebrities) and .88 (weight of a cat). Mean relative anchor distances also differed between
studies and was thus confounded sample size (and standard error). Note that the relative distance
between the anchor and the true value is an important moderator of anchoring effect strength
(e.g., Chapman & Johnson, 1994).

Test for Questionable Research Practices
          The reported effects were subjected to the same critical standard as the moderators, that
is, I report the funnel plot and p-curve analysis results (analysis code and data available at
https://osf.io/n9cy6/). Funnel plots are commonly used to determine publication bias. As all
effects are reported, the funnel plot for the anchoring effects should be symmetrical. There is no
symmetry of effect sizes as visible in Figure 13 and indicated by an Egger’s test, t(22) = 6.08, p
< .001.
Figure 13
Funnel plot of the 24 anchoring effects from the three studies included in this research
          In order to explain the asymmetry of the funnel plot, exploratory analyses were
conducted. They revealed that the standard error (sample size) and the relative anchor distance
are confounded between studies. That is, the sample size was smaller for the studies which

of evidential value (all tests for flatness p > .999), estimated power of 1-β = .99, 95% CI = [.99,

content.content:
# Citers of OpAQ (10.5334/jopd.67) and meta-analysis (10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn): novelty check

Sources: OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar (OpAQ DOI only; S2 does not index wf2tn by DOI, title search rate-limited), Google Scholar cited-by via SerpAPI (OpAQ cluster 5670922102386136969, 7 citers; wf2tn clusters 9079720239863130570 and 5707472742057289217, 14 + 3 citers, all retrieved), web search. No data files opened. Page refs = PDF pages.

## Bottom line
No citer relates the two-anchor proportional AI to anchor extremity on OpAQ human item-level estimates, and none fits process models to them. The only reuse of OpAQ human estimates is Röseler et al. 2024 Meta-Psychology (reliability). Two LLM papers reuse OpAQ items only. wf2tn has no published version (OpenAlex/Crossref/GS). OpAQ OSF wiki (ygnvb) names "effects of anchor extremeness" as a testable hypothesis and lists no publications using the dataset. Closest prior work uses own data: Barrera-Lemarchand 2024 (one-sided weight falls with distance, r = -.56), Mayer & Rebholz 2024 (not an OpAQ citer), and the unpublished Röseler & Wagner OSF project dsyrk (anchor distance vs effect strength, 2020-21, no write-up).

## Priority 1: Barrera-Lemarchand et al. 2024, Psych Sci, 10.1177/09567976241252138 (CITED-ONLY, own data)
Read: author-accepted Word manuscript (49 pp., Apr 2024; preprint 10.31234/osf.io/wvfm3). Page refs are manuscript pages; published typeset version not verified.
- OpAQ items/data: NOT used. OpAQ only in refs (MS p. 31); "Röseler et al., 2022" cited in text for the "anchoring extremeness effect" (pp. 6, 8, 15). Barrera-Lemarchand, Navajas, Freira are OpAQ co-authors (Correction), so their data likely feed OpAQ.
- Model (MS p. 8, Eq. 4): anchored mean mu_j = w_j*A_j + (1-w_j)*mu, with w_j = w0 * exp(-beta*|A_j - theta|); theta = true value, beta = sensitivity to anchor-truth distance ("anchoring extremeness effect"). Simulation: theta=324, mu=250, A_L=10, A_H=1000, w0=1, beta=0.0017.
- Exp 2 design (MS pp. 13-14): N = 396 online, Argentina; 30 percentage questions (0-100), two sets of 15 (Group 1 n=119, Group 2 n=277); fixed anchors 5% (low) and 95% (high) for all questions; low/high assignment random per question; control group unanchored; 20 s per question; preregistered aspredicted RYC_4Y5.
- Distance: raw |A_j - theta| in percentage points, not normalised. Anchors fixed, so distance varies only via theta. Fig. 3D (caption MS p. 17): weight per question (blue = low, red = high anchor) vs distance, log scale on weight, linear fit.
- Anchoring weight (SI p. 43, Eq. 16): w_j = (mu_j - mu)/(A_j - mu), one-sided per anchor and per question, against unanchored mean mu; called "very similar" to Jacowitz-Kahneman index (MS p. 15). 0 = no effect, 1 = mean equals anchor. NOT the two-anchor AI.
- Result (MS p. 16): r = -0.56, p = 3e-6 between weight and |A - theta| (n not stated; ~60 points = 30 questions x 2 anchors is my inference). Supporting (MS pp. 14-15): true value < 50% (17 questions): low-anchor group not different from truth, t(16)=0.95, p=.36, BF01=2.7; > 50% (13 questions): high-anchor group t(12)=2.01, p=.07.
- Model comparison (MS p. 16): exponential best; vs linear dAIC = dBIC = 1.9; vs hyperbolic w0/(1+beta|A-theta|) (their Eq. 7) dAIC = dBIC = 0.59. Weak discrimination. Single symmetric weight per question beats separate low/high weights (dAIC 1.6, dBIC 5.7).

## Priority 2: Mayer & Rebholz 2024, PsyArXiv 10.31234/osf.io/69jwr (does NOT cite OpAQ; full text read; no journal version found)
- Random-dot estimation (100-599 dots; 25 anchoring images) (p. 11). 2 expertise x 2 relevance x 2 extremity; extremity = anchors deviating +/-35% ("low") vs +/-70% ("high") from truth, coded -0.5/0.5 (p. 14). Preregistered aspredicted GZQ_48M.
- DV: absolute relative error = |judgment/correct*100 - 100| (p. 14).
- Exp 1 extremity: beta = 4.88 pp, 95% CI [2.80, 6.97], t(23.79) = 4.60, p < .001 (p. 15). Exp 2: beta = 7.37, [4.53, 10.20], t(24.00) = 5.09, p < .001 (p. 21).
- Exploratory (Exp 1): relative error on signed anchor deviation beta = 0.15 [0.09, 0.21], t(23.08) = 5.13 (page not pinned, ~p. 17).
- My reading, not the authors': doubling anchor distance (35% -> 70%) adds ~5-7 points of error, i.e. ~0.14-0.21 per unit extra distance: roughly constant proportional pull. "Stronger anchoring" is absolute, not proportional.

## All citing works
| # | Work (source) | Class | Summary |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Röseler et al. 2024, Correction, JOPD, 10.5334/jopd.92 (OA, S2, GS) | n/a | Author list only: 10 co-authors omitted "due to an administrative error" (p. 2). No item/trial/variable changes. |
| 2 | Röseler, Weber, Helgerth, Stich et al. 2024, Meta-Psychology 8, 10.15626/MP.2022.3236 (OA, GS) | REUSED-OPAQ (human estimates) | Reliability of person-level scores: 41 studies, N = 9,825, median 6 items (p. 5). Mean interitem r = .126 (REML .137 [.078, .197]); 0-1 score .131, restricted .164, adjustment .154 (pp. 5-6). 0-1 score = (estimate - anchor)/(true - anchor) (p. 4): proportional, per person, never related to distance. Aside: nonlinear models for extreme anchors "likely more precise" (p. 11). |
| 3 | Röseler, Incerti, Rebholz, Seida, Papenmeier, Meta-Psychology 9 (2025), 10.15626/MP.2024.4137 (Crossref-verified; preprint jztk2 v1-v3) | CITED-ONLY (contributes data) | TOTE formalisation, adjustment = floor(t/pause)*strength (p. 3). 4 studies N = 898: r_time = 0.02 [-.045, .086]; r_anchoring = 0.191 [-.211, .594], Q(8) = 177.61 (p. 22). Proposes bidirectional adjustment (p. 22). Studies 1, 2, 4 data in OpAQ (p. 24). |
| 4 | Mayer & Heck 2025, PBR 32:1142-1164, 10.3758/s13423-024-02619-9 (OA, GS) | CITED-ONLY (wf2tn) | Sequential collaboration model; anchoring A = E_i*(y_prev - T): fixed fraction of anchor-truth gap, implies distance-invariant AI (p. 1147, Eq. 9). No OpAQ. |
| 5 | Fischer, Mayer, Kimmerle 2026, JBDM, 10.1002/bdm.70063 (OA, GS) | CITED-ONLY (wf2tn) | Judgment invariance in sequential collaboration; cites wf2tn for "informative anchors induce a higher anchoring effect". |
| 6 | Onuki & Ueda 2025, Commun Psychol 3:97, 10.1038/s44271-025-00276-9 (OA, S2, GS) | CITED-ONLY (OpAQ co-authors) | Range nudges. OpAQ cited for robustness (p. 1); wf2tn g = 0.59 (speed), g = 0.94 (duration) for power (pp. 2-5). |
| 7 | Barrera-Lemarchand et al. 2024 (OA, S2, GS) | CITED-ONLY | See Priority 1. |
| 8 | Reimer et al. 2024, Sustainability, 10.3390/su16062540 (OA, GS) | CITED-ONLY (wf2tn) | N = 384; current temperature, scale midpoint and range affect setpoints; increment does not (abstract). |
| 9 | Navarre, Didierjean, Thomas 2024, Année psychologique 124:591-634, 10.3917/anpsy1.244.0591 (OA, GS) | CITED-ONLY (review) | Claims anchor/effect relation is nonlinear beyond plausible range, high anchors only; low anchors linear (p. 597; p. 602). Cites Chapman & Johnson 1994, Thorsteinson 2011, row 2 (which does not show this). Weaker effects for implausible anchors (p. 598). |
| 10 | Young, Speekenbrink et al. 2026, Cogn Psychol 164:101796, 10.1016/j.cogpsych.2026.101796 (OA, GS) | CITED-ONLY (wf2tn) | Cited pp. 1, 18. Own studies; no OpAQ data. |
| 11 | Stöcker 2024 thesis, 10.20378/irb-96573 (OA) | CITED-ONLY (wf2tn) | Advice taking; p. 23. |
| 12 | Shiddieqi et al. 2024, Scientax, 10.52869/st.v5i2.667 (OA) | CITED-ONLY (wf2tn) | Tax compliance; reference list only. |
| 13 | Owusu, Wiegreffe, Feldman 2026, arXiv 2606.12818 (S2) | REUSED-OPAQ (items only) | 100 OpAQ questions to 9-option multiple choice; LLM circuit localisation (pp. 1, 3). No extremity analysis. |
| 14 | Owusu & Feldman 2026, ACL short, 10.18653/v1/2026.acl-short.16 (S2) | REUSED-OPAQ (items only) | 50 OpAQ items, replicated on 99 (1,188 obs.); anchoring measured as TVD / expected-value shift; falls with model confidence, beta ~ -0.05, p < .001 (pp. 2-3). |
| 15 | Vaccaro 2026, SSRN, 10.2139/ssrn.6732238 (S2) | CITED-ONLY | LLM spec curve, 2,430 configs; anchor distance high/medium/low is one factor; indices from negative to > 1.0; OpAQ cited for "human range 0.3-0.6" (pp. 13-14). |
| 16 | Rebholz, Groß, Röseler, Stage 1 RR, PsyArXiv 5u8br (v2 2025 read; v3 10.31234/osf.io/5u8br_v3, Feb 2026) (GS) | CITED-ONLY (OpAQ summary for power) | Anchoring data = Weber & Röseler 2025 (p. 20); OpAQ Shiny d = 0.60 [0.58, 0.78] for power (p. 28). "extremely high or low anchors tend to lead to smaller effects" (p. 6). |
| 17 | Rebholz, Biella, Hütter, JBDM 2024, 10.1002/bdm.2369 (GS only) | Probable GS mis-link | OpAQ absent from preprint text (x36az) and JBDM Crossref refs. Method point: ratio indices (incl. anchoring index) assume linearity; regression weights allow nonlinear distance terms. |
| 18 | Weber & Röseler 2025, EJOP 21(1), 10.5964/ejop.9891 (web) | Contributes data; OpAQ for power only | N = 78, 18 items; power from OpAQ score correlations (27 Aug 2021) (p. 2). |
| 19 | Röseler 2023 z-curve, MetaArXiv 10.31222/osf.io/ewb2t (GS) | CITED-ONLY, NOT READ | Replication-rate prediction. |
| 20 | Haidinger et al. 2026, EJOR, 10.1016/j.ejor.2026.06.002 (GS) | CITED-ONLY, NOT READ | Multi-criteria decision effort. |
| 21 | Edmar, Enquist, Luke 2025, misinformation meta-analysis, PsyArXiv m68kf (GS) | CITED-ONLY, NOT READ | Different topic. |
| 22 | Röseler et al. 2024, JCRE, 10.18718/81781.38 (GS; DataCite-verified) | CITED-ONLY | Replication of Epley & Gilovich moderators. |

Checked, do not cite OpAQ: Lou et al. arXiv 2412.06593; "Anchors in the Machine" arXiv 2511.05766. Schley & Weingarten 2026 Management Science 10.1287/mnsc.2023.03238 cites neither work (90 Crossref refs).

## Röseler anchoring works 2022-2026
- OpAQ: JOPD 2022, 10.5334/jopd.67. Correction 2024, 10.5334/jopd.92.
- Hanging the Anchor Off a New Ship (Röseler & Schütz): preprint only, 10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn. OSF file qswer = OpAQ_metaanalysis_v1.pdf.
- Measurements of Susceptibility to Anchoring are Unreliable: preprint b6t35 (2022); Meta-Psychology 2024, 10.15626/MP.2022.3236.
- Testing the Reliability of Anchoring Susceptibility Scores (Weber & Röseler): preprint 2kfh3 (2022); EJOP 2025, 10.5964/ejop.9891. Unpublished corrected version Preprint_Corrigendum.pdf (Jan 2026, OSF component sz5b9) with corrected script/data (Aug-Dec 2025). Corrected Table 1 reassigns item effect sizes, e.g. Danube -0.32 -> 1.12; Russia-US distance 1.24 -> -0.32; lottery 0.89 -> -0.26 (published p. 4 vs corrected p. 10). Cause not stated. Unknown whether OpAQ master file (ygnvb, last modified 2023-11-22) has the corrected item mapping; relevant for item-level analysis.
- Falsifying the Insufficient Adjustment Model: preprint jztk2 (2023; v2/v3 2025); Meta-Psychology 9 (2025), 10.15626/MP.2024.4137.
- Replicating Epley & Gilovich: preprint bgp3m (2022); JCRE 2024, 10.18718/81781.38.
- Assimilation and Contrast are Everywhere (Röseler & Schütz): preprint 2024, 10.31234/osf.io/krwcn. Theory review; distance only via Sherif et al. 1958 (p. 5) and Chapman & Johnson (pp. 10, 13). No OpAQ analysis.
- Assimilation to External Cues (Rebholz, Groß, Röseler): Stage 1 RR, v3 Feb 2026, 10.31234/osf.io/5u8br_v3.
- PREreview of "Anchoring-Based Causal Design (ABCD)": Zenodo 2026, 10.5281/zenodo.21281801. NOT READ.
- "Absolute versus Relative Adjustment from Anchors" (Röseler & Wagner), OSF project dsyrk: created Oct 2020; OpenAlex 2026 date = last-modified date. Wiki: "data and analyses that explored the relationship between anchor distance and anchor effect strength." File names only (not opened): simulation_absrel_v5.R (Dec 2020), two pretests (Nov-Dec 2020), main study (analysis scripts Jan 2021), reanalysis script for Teovanović 2015. No manuscript; no write-up found anywhere.
- "Anchoring Effects Meta Analysis", OSF project 63um5: wiki says withdrawn; replaced by the mega-analysis (= wf2tn). Only 2021 preregistration materials.

content.content:
# Novelty check: anchoring extremity x proportional anchoring index (tasks A-D)

## Bottom line

No paper from 2022-2026 was found that does all three of the following:

- compute the proportional anchoring index (AI) item by item on OpAQ;
- relate the AI to anchor extremity, scaled by the true value or by uncertainty;
- compare the result against simulated predictions from process models.

The closest pieces:

- Röseler & Schütz (2022): OpAQ data, 386 items, extremity relative to the true value, outcome Hedges g.
- The Schley & Weingarten meta-study (Jan 2025 version only): 8 items, anchors at calibration percentiles, z-scored outcome.
- Lieder et al. (2018a): fitted the AI for 15 Jacowitz & Kahneman items, but never tested how the AI varies with extremity.

Both empirical extremity findings are larger absolute or standardized gaps. A constant AI would also produce a larger gap when anchors are further apart. So neither tests proportional adjustment; an AI-based analysis is the discriminating test.

Tier labels:

- **full text**: read in full.
- **figure-read**: my estimate from a plot.
- **abstract only**: only the abstract was read.
- **UNVERIFIED**: not read.

Closeness to the planned study is rated 0-3. All DOIs were verified via api.crossref.org, and title and authors match. No data files were opened.

## A. Schley & Weingarten

### Versions

This is one paper in several versions.

- **Management Science:** doi 10.1287/mnsc.2023.03238, "Fifty Years of Anchoring Effects: A Theoretical Reintegration and Meta-Analysis", Schley & Weingarten. Crossref gives a published-online date of 2026-05-19, with no volume, issue or pages yet. I did not read the published text (UNVERIFIED).
- **PsyArXiv teq7k_v2 (2025-12-09):** Crossref marks it `is-preprint-of` the Management Science DOI. Its abstract is identical to the journal abstract, and SSRN 10.2139/ssrn.5893864 matches it. Read in full (48 pp.). This is the basis for the page references below.
- **PsyArXiv teq7k v1, primary file revision 5 (2025-01-27) = SSRN 10.2139/ssrn.5114456:** "50 Years of Anchoring: A Meta-Analysis and Meta-Study of Anchoring Effects". Read in full (88 pp.). It adds a preregistered meta-study (N = 1,968). That meta-study is absent from v2 and, judging by the abstract, from the Management Science version.
- **SSRN 10.2139/ssrn.4605057 (2023):** earlier version with 1,283 effect sizes and g = 0.824 (abstract only).
- Online Appendices A-I (osf.io/d583s) were not read (UNVERIFIED).

### (1) Data sources

- 1,280 high-vs-low effect sizes, from 482 studies in 178 papers, after 23 Cook's-distance exclusions from 1,303 (v2, pp. 17 and 23).
- 2,601 effect sizes across all databases (abstract).
- Database searches were run in Dec 2017, Feb 2019 and Feb 2024. Many Labs 1 and 2 and the Reproducibility Project were added (pp. 15-16).
- **OpAQ is not used and not cited.** The only Röseler reference is the 2021 subliminal-anchoring paper.

### (2) How extremity was coded

- **Meta-analysis:** a binary "Extreme Anchors" flag, set when the original authors defined the anchor as "extreme" or "implausible", or when there were other, more moderate anchor levels. Example: in O'Conor et al. 1999, the $100 and $100,000 anchors are coded extreme. k = 49 of 1,280 (Table 2, pp. 20-21).
  - There is no measure relative to the true value, SD or percentiles.
  - Only 8.3% of studies (40 of 482) reported a calibration pretest (p. 39).
- **Meta-study (2025 version only):** calibration percentiles from a Prolific sample, at 3rd/97th, 15th/85th and 30th/70th. Varied within participants over 8 items (Table 7, p. 50). This is effectively extremity relative to uncertainty.

### (3) Level of testing and results

**Meta-analysis** (effect-size level, 3-level random-effects model with effect sizes nested in studies, robust variance estimation, v2 p. 22):

| Model | Estimate |
|---|---|
| Multivariate | -0.02 [-0.20, 0.16] |
| With controls | -0.02 [-0.19, 0.15] |
| Univariate | 0.01 [-0.18, 0.20] |
| Within-study subset | 0.09 [-0.14, 0.31] |

- Source for the table: Table 5, p. 28.
- Table 6 (p. 29): g = 0.84 [0.65, 1.03] for extreme vs 0.82 [0.76, 0.88] for not extreme. In the within-study subset: 0.69 (k = 29) vs 0.61 (k = 33).
- Quote (p. 31): "this coefficient implies not that the anchoring effect is proportional to the anchor extremity but that the total magnitude of the anchoring effect appears no larger or smaller for anchors defined by their study's authors as 'extreme.'" They add that the coding may not capture the latent construct.
- No test for nonlinearity.

**Meta-study** (trial level, mixed model, 2025 version pp. 52-54):

- Estimates were winsorized and z-scored within item.
- The model has item dummies, linear extremity coding (-0.5/0/0.5), quadratic coding, and interactions with the anchor condition.
- The text gives no numbers. Figure 4 (p. 55, figure-read): extremity linear x anchoring effect about +0.74; quadratic about +0.10, CI above 0.
- Figure 3 (p. 53, figure-read): the high-minus-low gap is about 0.2 SD at 30/70, 0.5 SD at 15/85 and 1.0 SD at 3/97.
- Quote (p. 56): "results of the meta-study indicated a large increase in the anchoring effect when the anchors were more extreme."
- This is not a proportional-AI finding. The distance between the two anchors widens several-fold across levels, e.g. African countries 24/48 vs 3/72 and Kalam 45/60 vs 20/80 (Table 7). The AI cannot be computed from the paper.
- Quote (2025 version, p. 70): a better design "requires assessing anchor values at each level of a baseline distribution – rather than at just the 3rd/97th, 15th/85th, and 30th/70th percentiles."

### (4) Effect-size metric

- Hedges g only (v2 p. 18).
- Separate databases for control-condition comparisons (N = 537), correlations (N = 228) and anchor-estimate gaps (375 raw, 204 standardized). These are all in the appendices (p. 19, UNVERIFIED).
- No AI or other unitless adjustment metric appears in any version.

### (5) Theories compared, and how

- Seven theories: anchoring-and-adjustment, numeric priming, selective accessibility, attitudinal perspective, scale distortion, extremeness aversion, and noise theory.
- Qualitative predictions are coded in Table 1 (p. 7).
- Extremity predictions (p. 12):
  - anchoring-and-adjustment: increase up to a threshold;
  - selective accessibility: increase up to a threshold;
  - attitudinal perspective (Wegener et al. 2001): inverted U;
  - extremeness aversion: increase;
  - noise theory: increase.
- No model fitting. Quote (p. 33): "Instead of counting up winners and losers, we instead take a broader reflection on each theory."
- Evaluation of extremeness aversion (p. 35): "meta-analytic evidence reveals no reliable extremity moderation."
- They call for formal models, citing Turner & Schley 2016 and Lieder et al. 2018 (p. 39).

### (6) Random or uninformative anchors

- "Transparently random" (Table 5, p. 28):
  - multivariate -0.19** [-0.33, -0.05];
  - with controls -0.23** [-0.39, -0.07];
  - univariate -0.05 [-0.18, 0.07];
  - within-study subset -0.18 [-1.90, 1.53].
- Table 6 (p. 29): g = 0.78 [0.65, 0.91] random vs 0.83 [0.77, 0.90] not random.
- The 2025 version reports -0.27*** multivariate (p. 42).
- Primed or incidental anchors: -0.72*** [-0.88, -0.56] (p. 28). Univariate g = 0.16 [0.08, 0.24] (Table 6, p. 29).

### Closeness

- Meta-analysis: 1.
- Meta-study: 2. Extremity is relative to uncertainty, but there are only 8 items, the outcome is z-scored, there is no AI, and no models are simulated.

## B. Young et al. 2026

"Anchoring the anchor: judgments of both items assimilate in item-based anchoring", Cognitive Psychology 164, 101796, doi 10.1016/j.cogpsych.2026.101796. Full text read: CC-BY copy from the Cambridge repository, with journal pagination.

- **Design:** 10 studies, N = 1,353 after exclusions (pp. 7-8), plus 953 calibration participants. Items serve as anchors: "Does a torch cost more or less than a laptop?"
- **Outcome:** percentile rank of each estimate within the calibration distribution, following Jacowitz & Kahneman, plus an assimilation score (p. 7).
- **Result:** meta-analytic g = 0.25 [0.05, 0.45] (p. 11). Low-value items were anchored more than high-value items (the hypothesis that more variable items would be anchored more was not supported).
- **OpAQ:** not used. Röseler & Schütz 2022 is cited only as a meta-analysis (p. 1).
- **Models:** no computational model fitted. The only simulation validates the rank measure (Supplementary Material 1). They conclude that selective accessibility gives the best account (abstract).
- **Extremity:** only a discussion remark. Study 1 had the largest effect, and its item values differed by factors of 44-500. They call this "in line with" Lieder et al. (pp. 15-16). No proportional-adjustment analysis.
- **Discrepancy:** they cite Schley & Weingarten (2025) as d = 0.876 (p. 2) and 0.88 (p. 15). Every Schley & Weingarten version I read reports 0.824 or 0.825. Not resolved.
- **Closeness: 0.**

## C. Searches, 2022-2026

**Method:**

- OpenAlex lists of 2022-2026 citers: Lieder 2018a (164), Lieder 2018b (21), Turner & Schley (54), OpAQ jopd.67 (4).
- OpenAlex keyword searches and web searches.
- The OpAQ citer list is low-recall: it missed two papers that do use OpAQ.

**No citer fits process models to multi-item anchoring data or relates the proportional AI to extremity.**

| Paper (verified DOI) | What it did | Close |
|---|---|---|
| **Röseler & Schütz 2022, "Hanging the Anchor Off a New Ship: A Meta-Analysis of Anchoring Effects", PsyArXiv 10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn** (single version, 2022-03-09; unpublished) | Full text. Meta-analysis **of OpAQ**: 90 studies, k = 386 items, N = 17,708; outcome Hedges g (pp. 17-18). Overall g = 0.689 [0.589, 0.789] (abstract). Extremity = mean relative distance of anchor from the true value per item (p. 11). "Relative distance" b = 0.040, k = 312, p < .001 (Table 2, p. 21). They call the relationship "positive and nonlinear" (Table 4, p. 29; p. 30), but the PDF shows only a linear coefficient; the nonlinear evidence may be in their online app (UNVERIFIED). Random anchors: smaller effects, still above 0 (p. 26). Explicit call (p. 34): a unitless "relative strength of adjustment" metric "could help to formalize the relationship between anchor distance and adjustment strength." | **2** |
| Röseler, Weber, Helgerth & Stich 2024, "Measurements of Susceptibility to Anchoring are Unreliable", Meta-Psychology 8, 10.15626/mp.2022.3236 | Abstract only. Built on OpAQ; individual susceptibility scores are unreliable. No extremity or model analysis. | 1 |
| Röseler, Incerti, Rebholz & Seida 2025, "Falsifying the Insufficient Adjustment Model", PsyArXiv 10.31234/osf.io/jztk2_v3 | Abstract only. Formalized insufficient-adjustment model; 4 studies, N = 898. Reducing adjustment time did not bring estimates closer to the anchor. | 1 |

## D. What Lieder 2018 and Turner & Schley 2016 fitted

Page numbers for both Lieder papers are from the 2017 PsyArXiv preprints (osf 5x2em and zu4pt). The published PBR pagination was not checked.

### Lieder et al. 2018a, PBR 25:322-349, doi 10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8

- **Jacowitz & Kahneman AI, 15 quantities.**
  - Setup: sigma from their own elicitation; mu from Jacowitz & Kahneman's unanchored medians; 2 parameters fitted by least squares on the AI; 29 adjustments, step size 22.4 (p. 25).
  - **Predicted mean AI 53.22% vs observed 48.48%**; item-level r(13) = 0.62, p = .0135 (p. 26).
  - Predicted AI correlates with sigma: Spearman rho = 0.586, p = .024. This matches Jacowitz & Kahneman's r(13) = -0.68 between confidence and AI (p. 31).
- **Epley & Gilovich 2006, self-generated anchors, 19 quantities:** relative adjustment 80.62% predicted vs 80.95% observed; r(17) = 0.61 (p. 27).
- **Cognitive load:** r(5) = 0.96 (p. 29).
- **Russo & Schoemaker 1989 (Attila, anchors 500-1300 in 200-year bins), plus MTurk replication (N = 300):** simulated with the Jacowitz & Kahneman parameters. Mean estimates rise linearly with the anchor; the model overshoots at the highest anchor. Compared on mean estimates, not AI (pp. 30-31).
- **Simmons et al. 2010 Study 3b:** incentives affect adjustment only for implausible anchors.
  - Plausible: 0.76 [-0.42, 1.94].
  - Implausible: 17.8 [9.76, 25.91].
  - rho(22) = 0.72 (p. 39).
- **Stated prediction:** bias is at most about (a - x)·r^t, so bias grows in proportion to the anchor-truth distance. That means a constant relative adjustment for a fixed number of adjustments t (Eqs. 3-4, p. 20; Table 1, p. 23).
- **Their Fig. 4 (p. 19), my reading, not stated in their text:**
  - the optimal number of adjustments rises with distance in sigma units;
  - at intermediate time costs, the remaining bias is non-monotonic in distance, which implies the AI could fall with extremity.
- The AI-by-extremity relationship was never derived or tested.

### Lieder et al. 2018b, PBR 25:775-784, doi 10.3758/s13423-017-1288-6

- Bus-delay prediction with time-cost x error-cost incentives.
- Exp 1: N = 30 recruited, self-generated anchor (p. 6). Exp 2: N = 60, provided low/high anchors (p. 14).
- Bias modelled as linear in the true value.
- Relative adjustment: 41.3% [38.5, 44.0] in Exp 1 (p. 10). In Exp 2, 29.86% for low and 27.25% for high anchors, not different (z = 1.16; p. 16).
- One quantity; no extremity manipulation.

### Turner & Schley 2016, Cognitive Psychology 90:1-47, doi 10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003

Full text from the author's website, journal pagination.

- **Exp 1:** N = 589 across 5 between-participant conditions: unanchored prior, regular, directional, irrelevant, cognitive load (p. 12).
  - 6 items from Simmons et al. and Jacowitz & Kahneman, with **one anchor per item** (high for items 1, 3, 5; low for items 2, 4, 6; p. 13).
  - Fitted per item with Bayesian estimation (p. 14).
  - **No AI is possible with this design, and none is used.**
- **Exp 2:** N = 189, within-person prior and posterior estimates plus confidence ratings; hierarchical model (p. 26).
- **Extremity is an assumption, not a finding.**
  - Anchor influence k is mapped from "prior consistency" w (the prior CDF at the anchor; p. 21) through a Bézier curve.
  - Quote (p. 23): the mapping produces "an inverted U-shaped relationship between anchor extremity and the magnitude of the shift… For simplicity." An asymptote is allowed via k_max.
  - Summary (p. 25): more implausible anchors have "a proportionally smaller influence".
- Fig. 14 (p. 31) shows a curvilinear pattern across participants' prior-to-anchor distance for one fixed anchor per item. This is not a test across anchor levels.
- Practical aim of choosing "optimal" anchors (p. 35).

### Closeness

- Lieder 2018a: 1-2 (source of a model, not a test).
- Lieder 2018b: 0-1.
- Turner & Schley 2016: 1.

content.content:
# Anchoring vs anchor extremity: quantitative evidence from primary texts

AI = (est_high − est_low) / (anchor_high − anchor_low) (Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995), computed on means unless stated.
"Local slope" = change in estimate / change in anchor between adjacent anchor levels.
All arithmetic: `/tmp/jdmsim/scratch_nov_classic_ai.py` (output `_ai_out.txt`). Notes: `_findings.md`.
DOIs verified via api.crossref.org (title + first author match) unless marked otherwise. No data files opened.

Provenance tags: FULL = full text read; FIG = figures only; ABS = abstract only; SECONDARY = numbers from another source (named); UNVERIFIED = not checked against the primary source.

## 1. Chapman & Johnson 1994, JBDM 7:223–242, doi 10.1002/bdm.3960070402 — FIG
- Full text not obtained (Wiley paywall). Exhibit images from the author's academia.edu upload; values read off figures (±1). Abstract (Wiley page): "implausibly extreme anchors had a proportionally smaller effect than anchors close to the expected value".
- Exp 1: selling prices for 16 lotteries (4 EVs × 4 payoff ranges; Exhibit 2). Anchors = 0.1, 0.7, 1.3, 1.9 × EV.
- Exhibit 3 (p.229): geometric-mean prices ≈ 74, 106.5, 127, 127.5. Anchors scaled by geometric-mean EV 137.6 → 13.8, 96.3, 178.8, 261.4.
  - Local slopes: 32.5/82.5 = 0.39; 20.5/82.5 = 0.25; 0.5/82.5 = 0.006.
  - AI moderate pair (0.7/1.3) = 0.25; AI extreme pair (0.1/1.9) = 53.5/247.5 = 0.22.
  - Saturation at the high end only (high/low asymmetry).
- Exhibit 4 (p.230), by payoff range (extremity relative to plausible range):
  - very narrow (extreme anchors far outside range): ≈ 84 / 104 / 122 / 111 → inverted U
  - narrow: ≈ 67 / 98 / 104 / 132 → monotone
  - wide: ≈ 63 / 106 / 143 / 137; very wide: ≈ 83 / 117 / 137 / 123 → downturn at 1.9
- Exp 2, Exhibit 6 (p.234): monetary anchors 1.08–28.16 × EV → prices ≈ 182 / 248 / 297 / 344, monotone. AI not computable (multipliers per level in unread text; UNVERIFIED).
- Implication: AI falls modestly with extremity; raw effect saturates or turns down when anchors lie far outside the plausible range.

## 2. Strack & Mussweiler 1997, JPSP 73:437–446, doi 10.1037/0022-3514.73.3.437 — FULL
- Study 3: n = 67, 8 items, within-subject 2 (high/low) × 2 (plausible/implausible). Plausible anchors ≈ 1 SD from the calibration mean (n = 151); implausible > 10 SD (Table 5, p.442).
- Table 6 (p.443), z-scored estimates: plausible high .04 / low −.13 (diff .17 SD); implausible high .25 / low −.17 (diff .42 SD). Interaction F(1,66) = 3.55, p < .07.
- Implied: raw shift ≈ 2.5× larger over an anchor gap > 10× wider → AI ≈ ¼ or less. Caveat: z standardised on the study's own responses, not calibration SD.
- Appendix (p.446) per-item raw means: median AI plausible 0.25, implausible 0.06 (implausible anchor gaps 7–132× wider). Einstein, Gandhi and Da Vinci-implausible rows are internally implausible (e.g., Einstein means ≈ 1807 with anchors 1905/1939); likely typographical. Do not rely on per-item values.
- Implication: larger raw effect but much smaller AI for implausible anchors.

## 3. Mussweiler & Strack 2001, Social Cognition 19:145–160, doi 10.1521/soco.19.2.145.20705 — FULL
- 4 anchor levels per item; both implausible anchors high.
- Study 1, Antarctic mean temp (true −68 °C; Table 1, p.154; n 15–16/cell): anchors −43, −17 (±1 SD), 700, 900 (≈ 56 and 72 SD) → means −41.12, −24.84, −23.27, −24.44.
  - AI plausible = 16.28/26 = 0.63; AI implausible = −1.17/200 = −0.006 (within noise); AI −43→700 = 17.85/743 = 0.024.
- Study 2, Gandhi age (true 78; Table 2, p.156; n 26–28/cell): anchors 61, 86 (±1 SD), 214, 271 (≈ 18, 26 SD) → means 62.92, 70.36, 75.26, 72.86.
  - AI plausible = 7.44/25 = 0.30; AI implausible = −0.04; AI 61→214 = 0.08.
- One-sided AI with calibration mean inferred as midpoint of plausible pair (−30 °C; 73.5 yrs): Antarctic 0.86, 0.40, 0.009, 0.006; Gandhi 0.85, −0.25, 0.013, −0.003. Inference is shaky for Gandhi (SD implied by 61/86 ≈ 12.5 vs by "18 and 26 SD" ≈ 7.7).
- Implication: raw shift plateaus at the plausibility boundary → AI ≈ 1/distance beyond it.

## 4. Wegener, Petty, Detweiler-Bedell & Jarvis 2001, JESP 37:62–69, doi 10.1006/jesp.2000.1431 — FULL
- 8 items, 6 anchor levels each (Appendix, p.68); within-subject 2 × 2 (high/low × moderate/extreme); z-scored estimates.
- Exp 1A (n = 151): moderate +.50/−.52 (diff 1.02) vs extreme (e.g., Washington age 13/167) +.37/−.36 (0.73).
- Exp 1B (n = 145): moderate +.52/−.41 (0.93) vs very extreme (e.g., 2/167,054) +.15/−.25 (0.40).
- Exp 2 (n = 80, no "random anchor" instruction): moderate +.40/−.47 (0.87) vs very extreme +.26/−.19 (0.45). Plausibility 1.28 vs 4.38 (9-pt); rated plausibility mediated the extremity effect for low anchors (pp.65–66).
- Implied AI ratio extreme/moderate (illustrative: pooled z-diff ratio ÷ per-item anchor-gap ratio): 1A median ≈ 0.22 (0.05–0.26); 1B median ≈ 0.0015.
- Implication: raw effect inverted U; AI falls steeply.

## 5. Wegener, Petty, Blankenship & Detweiler-Bedell 2010, J Consumer Psych 20:5–16, doi 10.1016/j.jcps.2009.12.003 — FULL
- No new numbers. Footnote 1 (p.7), p.12 cite unpublished raw data (Wegener, Blankenship, Detweiler-Bedell & Petty 2009): 3 extremity levels, smaller effects at low and high than moderate extremity; downturn earlier for high-knowledge people. UNVERIFIED (unpublished).

## 6. Northcraft & Neale 1987, OBHDP 39:84–97, doi 10.1016/0749-5978(87)90046-x — FULL
- Listing-price anchors ±4% and ±12% of true value (Exp 1, p.88) or ±4%/±11% (Exp 2, p.92). Realtors said > 5% deviation is "obviously deviant".
- Exp 1 amateurs, appraisal (Table 1, p.89): anchors 65.9k / 71.9k / 77.9k / 83.9k → 63,571 / 67,452 / 70,423 / 72,196. Local slopes 0.65, 0.50, 0.30; AI moderate 0.50; AI extreme 8,625/18,000 = 0.48.
- Exp 1 experts, extreme anchors only (Table 2, p.90): AI = 7,379/18,000 = 0.41.
- Exp 2 (Tables 3–4, p.93), noisy: experts AI extreme 0.49, moderate −0.17; amateurs AI extreme 0.92, moderate 0.33. H2 (distant anchors less influential) not supported.
- Implication: within the plausible range (±12%), AI ≈ 0.5, roughly constant, mild concavity in Exp 1.

## 7. Jacowitz & Kahneman 1995, PSPB 21:1161–1166, doi 10.1177/01461672952111004 — SECONDARY
- Full text not obtained (SAGE paywall).
- Lieder et al. 2018 (manuscript p.17): empirical mean AI = 48.48% over 15 items; anchors at 15th/85th percentiles of calibration group. Lieder Fig. 7 plots per-item empirical AI.
- Per-item AIs and high/low asymmetry UNVERIFIED. Lieder Table C1 lists Lieder's own belief estimates (µ, σ) for J&K items, not J&K data.

## 8. Russo & Schoemaker 1989, Decision Traps (book, no DOI) — SECONDARY via Lieder et al. Fig. 10 (manuscript p.21)
- One item: year Attila defeated (true 451); anchor bins 500, 700, 900, 1100, 1300 (±100).
- Means read off figure ≈ 630, 680, 790, 885, 990 → local slopes 0.25, 0.55, 0.47, 0.53; overall 0.45; linear, no saturation ~850 years from truth.
- Lieder MTurk replication ≈ 590, 645, 870, 970, 1020 → top slope 0.25.

## 9. Lieder, Griffiths, Huys & Goodman 2018, PBR 25:322–349, doi 10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8 — FULL (preprint)
- Fixed number of adjustments (Eq. 4, p.13): E[x̂] = a·rᵗ + (1−rᵗ)·x → constant AI across extremity. R&S simulation with J&K-fitted parameters predicts slope ≈ 0.95 vs observed ≈ 0.45.
- Optimal number of adjustments (Fig. 4b, p.13; distance in σ units): near anchors barely adjusted, far anchors mostly adjusted away. Approx. bias/distance (figure readings): time cost ≈ 0.2 → 1.0, 0.85, 0.43, 0.18, 0.03 for 1σ–5σ; time cost ≈ 0.5 → 1.0, 0.98, 0.98, 0.63, 0.26.
- Implication: under optimal adjustment AI falls with extremity relative to uncertainty; raw bias non-monotone.

## 10. Turner & Schley 2016, Cognitive Psychology 90:1–47, doi 10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003 — FULL (lab-site PDF)
- Sec. 5.3.2 (pp.23–24), Fig. 9: mapping function builds in an inverted U between anchor extremity and posterior shift (citing Wegener 2001); parameter kmax allows an asymptote instead. Experiments use one anchor per item: no extremity data.

## 11. Hardt & Pohl 2003, Memory 11:379–394, doi 10.1080/09658210244000504 — ABS + SECONDARY
- Hindsight paradigm; anchor distance scaled to each participant's own range of plausible values.
- Abstract (PubMed 14562869): plausibility fell with distance; bias rose then fell; bias always higher for plausible anchors.
- Fig. 4 reproduced in Wilson, Arora, Zhang & Griffiths 2021 (Proc. 43rd CogSci; cocosci.princeton.edu/papers/wilson_rational.pdf), Fig. 1. Bias/distance at distances 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 7: anchor above estimate 0.12, 0.11, 0.14, 0.08, 0.03; below 0.38, 0.25, 0.17, 0.11, 0.06 (assumes shared units).
- Implication: raw shift inverted U; proportional shift falls with distance relative to own uncertainty.

## 12. Bystranowski, Janik, Próchnicki & Skórska 2021, Law & Human Behavior 45:1–23, doi 10.1037/lhb0000438 — FULL
- "Anchor value" = between-study z-score of anchor magnitude, binned at 25th/75th percentiles; not extremity relative to truth or uncertainty.
- Table 4 (p.12), control vs anchor: low k = 4 d = .43; medium k = 42 d = .59; high k = 5 d = .19; continuous coef −.04 (z′), −.08 (d), n.s.
- Table 5 (p.13), high vs low: low k = 5 d = .82; medium k = 25 d = 1.00; high k = 7 d = .77; continuous slope negative (text), n.s.
- p.17: moderate anchors largest effects, not significant.

## 13. Townson 2019, PhD dissertation, Michigan State Univ., doi 10.25335/p9dm-7a29 (DataCite verified) — ABS
- Meta-analysis, k = 84 r effect sizes, mean r = .401. "Extremity of the anchor was found to slightly weaken the impact." Size and coding UNVERIFIED (repository bot check blocked full text).

## 14. Harris et al. 2019, JEP:General 148:e30–e50, doi 10.1037/xge0000644 — FULL (accepted MS)
- Same items with different anchor gaps across experiments; means Table 2 (p.23).
- UK temperature: anchors 8/20 °C (p.17) → AI 2.02/12 = 0.17; anchors 2/25 °C (p.27) → 0.225 (Exp 3), 0.22 (Exp 5).
- UK car price: £6,000/£30,000 → 0.37; £13,000/£200,000 → 0.255.
- Internal inconsistency: p.26 describes Exp 1–2 anchors as 10/18 °C and £20,000; with 10/18 °C, temperature AI = 0.25.
- Implication: the two items move in opposite directions as the anchor gap widens.

## 15. Simmons, LeBoeuf & Nelson 2010, JPSP 99:917–932, doi 10.1037/a0021540 — FULL (Penn repository MS)
- Single anchor per item, plausible vs implausible (Tables 2–3, MS pp.47–48); no AI computable.
- Note 2 (MS p.42): implausible anchors left estimates further from truth on 6/8 items. Main finding: incentives increased adjustment only away from implausible anchors.

## 16. Schultze, Rakotoarisoa & Schulz-Hardt 2015, JDM 10:144–171, doi 10.1017/s1930297500003922 — FULL (advice-taking analogue)
- Exp 1 (Table 1, p.151): weight of advice = −0.093 − 0.003·d + 0.153·ln d (d = % distance) → ≈ 0.14 at 5%, 0.35 at 40–64%, 0.34 at 75%; peak ≈ 51% (my calculation from rounded coefficients).
- Pooled 6 experiments (pp.166–167): B1 = −0.002, B2 = 0.101; paper states peak at 63.84%; shallow far-distance downturn.
- Absolute opinion shift ≈ proportional to distance, no downturn up to 150%.
- Implication: proportional index inverted U, driven mainly by ignoring near advice; linear-plus-log form is a template for AI-vs-distance.

## 17. Marti & Wissler 2000, JEP:Applied 6:91–103, doi 10.1037/1076-898x.6.2.91 — ABS
- Abstract: awards rose with plaintiff request "but decreased with the most extreme request". Request levels $1.5M, $15M, $25M are SECONDARY (plaintiffmagazine.com).
- Conflict: Bystranowski et al. (p.6) cite this paper and Chapman & Bornstein 1996 as showing awards rising "even when the anchor is outlandishly high".

## 18. Other
- Thorsteinson 2011, JASP 41:1774–1792, doi 10.1111/j.1559-1816.2011.00779.x — ABS: both high implausible and extremely high anchors raised salary offers vs control; no comparison between them in the abstract.
- Lee, Lee & Kim 2022, Korean J Cognitive Science 33(1):77–93, doi 10.19066/cogsci.2022.33.1.004 (resolves via doi.org to KCI; not in Crossref) — ABS: extreme anchors smaller effects than plausible; difficult items larger effects.
- Smith, Windschitl & Bruchmann 2013, EJSP 43:97–108, doi 10.1002/ejsp.1921 — FULL: Fig. 3 (p.105) hypothesises a plateau reached earlier by high-knowledge people; not tested.
- Frederick & Mochon 2012, JEP:General 141:124–133, doi 10.1037/a0024006 — FULL: no extremity manipulation.
- Quattrone et al. 1984, unpublished (asymptote claim) — UNVERIFIED; cited in Wegener et al. 2001, p.63.
- Shanks, Barbieri-Hermitte & Vadillo 2020, Collabra, doi 10.1525/collabra.310: incidental anchors, not extremity.

## Not obtained (UNVERIFIED)
- Mussweiler & Strack 2000, doi 10.1006/jesp.1999.1414
- Thorsteinson et al. 2008, doi 10.1016/j.obhdp.2008.01.003
- LeBoeuf & Shafir 2006, doi 10.1002/bdm.535 (the brief's 10.1002/bdm.536 is a different paper); abstract does not mention extremity
- Mussweiler 2001, doi 10.1002/ejsp.52; abstract does not mention extremity
- Chapman & Bornstein 1996, doi 10.1002/(sici)1099-0720(199612)10:6<519::aid-acp417>3.0.co;2-5 (download tool returned a wrong paper; discarded)

## Synthesis

What the literature shows:
- Within the plausible range, AI is roughly flat: R&S slope ≈ 0.45; J&K mean AI ≈ 0.48; Northcraft & Neale 0.48–0.50; M&S 2001 plausible pairs 0.30–0.63; C&J moderate pair 0.25; Harris 0.17–0.37.
- At and beyond the plausibility boundary, the raw shift plateaus (M&S 2001; C&J high end) or declines (Wegener 1A/1B/2; Marti & Wissler abstract; Bystranowski high bin; Townson; Hardt & Pohl), so AI falls roughly as 1/distance.
- Counter-cases: S&M 1997 raw effect larger for implausible anchors (AI still smaller); Simmons note 2; C&J Exp 2 monotone rise over 1.08–28.16 × EV; Harris temperature AI rose with wider gap; C&J Exhibit 3 high/low asymmetry.

Stated theoretical curves:
- Linear / diminishing / contrast (inverted U): Chapman & Johnson Exhibit 1, p.225.
- Inverted U by assumption: Turner & Schley 2016.
- Asymptote: Mussweiler & Strack 2001; Quattrone et al. 1984.
- Constant AI (fixed adjustments) vs falling AI (optimal adjustments): Lieder et al. 2018.

Gaps the planned study fills:
- No study reports proportional AI across ≥ 3 levels spanning the plausibility boundary on many items with item-level means and a calibration SD. Nearest: C&J 1994 (lotteries; figures only), M&S 2001 (2 items; all-high implausibles), Northcraft & Neale (1 house per experiment; ±12% only), R&S (1 item; secondary).
- Only Hardt & Pohl scale distance to each person's own uncertainty (hindsight paradigm; secondary numbers).
- No study fits the competing models (resource-rational, anchor integration, insufficient adjustment, selective accessibility) to item-level AI-vs-extremity curves.
- Meta-analyses (Bystranowski, Townson) code extremity as raw magnitude or a crude category, not relative to truth or uncertainty.
